In multi-pass Energy Recovery Linacs (ERLs), multiple filling patterns can compete to affect beam-RF interactions and the electric field threshold. We analyze the effect of a simple uniform fill pattern where equal charges are placed in each bunch, comparing it to other patterns like the conventional filled ring structure. Using a single-value particle-in-cell electromagnetic simulator, we studied the impact of fill patterns on the beam-RF interactions in a 16-GHz 1 GeV linac with a 4-bunch fill. Our results show that the uniform fill pattern leads to the highest beam-RF power, reduces the energy loss per bunch by 13%, and raises the RF breakdown threshold current by 14% compared to the conventional fill pattern. Nonetheless, the uniform fill pattern also increases the required RF power by 13.8% due to lower charge injection per bunch. Our study ponders the potential benefits of non-conventional fill patterns in future high-energy ERLs. Our code, based on the General Particle Simulator (GPS), can be utilized for additional research on beam-RF interactions in various filling schemes and linac designs. Our numerical data is available for download at https://github.com/SLAC/UniformFillERL. Our analysis suggests that careful consideration of fill pattern design is necessary, potentially leading to significant improvements in high-energy ERLs. We propose several possible fill pattern optimizations, are planning further investigation into the potential benefits of non-uniform fill patterns, and encourage other researchers to explore this topic as well. Our simulation code can be utilized for additional research on beam-RF interactions in various filling schemes and linac designs, with the numerical data available for download at https://github.com/SLAC/UniformFillERL. Our analysis indicates that careful consideration of fill pattern design is necessary, potentially leading to significant improvements in high-energy ERLs, and we propose several possible fill pattern optimizations. Our research is applicable to future high-energy ERLs, and we encourage other researchers to explore this topic as well. Our simulation code is planned for utilization in the proposed 3-4 GeV Next Linear Collider, and we believe that our research can be beneficial for the development of future linear colliders. Our study also reveals that the impact of fill patterns on beam-RF interactions primarily results from the distribution of charge injection per bunch rather than the number of bunches itself. Consequently, we anticipate that our findings will be relevant to other future high-energy ERLs, such as the ILC-3 and ILC-4

Using modern amplitude methods, specifically the unitary on-shell method and the BCFW decomposition, we have completed a range of covariant components of two-gluon counterterms in QCD. These counterterms are part of a broader set of tools that can be used in collinear limits to predict counterterms for infrared divergences in $N=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, specifically for six-gluon amplitudes. We have also verified that these two-gluon counterterms match the predicted counterparts in QCD, supporting the status of counterterms as a consistent and universal infrared sector within $N=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. Furthermore, we have explored different gluon ordering combinations in BCFW decomposition, revealing that only certain, specifically constrained components contribute to counterterms. We investigated the free energy associated with stretching polymers in slabs of curved surfaces, taking into account the effects of surface defects and the non-zero thickness of the coating. Our analysis focuses on homogeneous brushes and reveals that the free energy can be divided into two components: the well-known energy related to stretching, and an additional energy influenced by the surface curvature. For homogenous brushes on a curved slab, the additional energy is directly proportional to the square of the mean radius of curvature, independent of the degree to which the chains are stretched. Moreover, we found that the mean distance between chains is affected by the curvature of the surface, and that the distribution of distances is asymptotically Rayleigh for large values of the mean. Numerical results demonstrate that the effects of surface defects become more pronounced as the degree of stretching increases. We also investigated brushes on shells and tubules, and found that the free energy can be described by a combination of energies associated with stretching, bending, and the compactness of the tube cross-sections. Our study provides a theoretical framework for understanding and predicting the properties of polymer brushes on surfaces with curvature and defects. It also highlights the importance of considering the coating thickness and the effects of surface defects on the free energy of stretching. Our results can be used to develop a unified approach to describing brush properties across a wide range of curvatures, from negative to positive values. This approach can be extended to investigate brushes on more complex surfaces with multiple curvatures, defects, and roughness. Our study also highlights the need for further research into modeling the free energy of bending in tubules and the compactness of tube cross-sections. It is essential to note that the effects of surface defects and the coating thickness depend on the degree of stretching, the mean distance between chains, and the shape of the brush. Our approach can be applied to various types of polymers, including DNA, proteins, and synthetic biopolymers, as well as different coating materials as long as the incompressibility condition holds. It is crucial to consider the effects of surface defects and the coating thickness on the free energy of stretching to accurately predict the properties and functionality of polymer brushes in various applications. It is also necessary to develop experimental techniques that can probe the free energy associated with bending and the compactness of tube cross-sections. Our approach can be used to design optimal brush structures and surface curvatures for specific functions and applications by manipulating the free energy components. It is the first study to investigate the effects of surface curvature on the free energy

Given a graph G = (V, E), the geodesic distance tractance problem involves finding the smallest integer k such that the metric dimension of a truncated version of G, obtained by removing edges with distance greater than k from the set of original vertices V, becomes 1. This involves formulating the problem as identifying the minimum value k such that the graph induced by removing edges with distance k > 1 from the original vertices has a metric dimension of 1. This formulation leads to a proof that this value k is equal to the minimum value required to reduce the metric dimension of G to 1. This value k can be determined as the minimum value such that the graph resulting from removing edges with distance greater than k from the original vertices V has a metric dimension of 1. This value k also has an alternative characterization as the minimum value such that the number of distinct representations of the vertices with respect to the metric dimension model reduces to 1. This value k is then analyzed in relation to its relationship with other graph parameters such as the minimum number of edges in a shortest path, the maximum number of edges in a shortest path, and the diameter of the truncated graph. This value k is observed to have a linear relationship with the minimum number of edges in a shortest path, the maximum number of edges in a shortest path, and the diameter of the truncated graph. This leads to an algorithm that determines the metric dimension of the truncated graph by analyzing its relationship with the minimum number of edges in a shortest path. This algorithm has an time complexity of $O(|E| + |V|\sqrt{|V|})$ for determining the metric dimension of the truncated graph. This value k is further analyzed in relation to its application in solving the minimum dominating set problem, the efficient metric generator problem, and the efficient dominant ordering problem. This leads to an algorithm that solves these problems on the truncated graph with a time complexity of $O(|E| + |V|\sqrt{|V|})$. This value k is then studied under the condition that the original graph G is a regular graph. This leads to an observation that the minimum value k is equal to the minimum value such that the number of distinct representations of the vertices with respect to the metric dimension model reduces to 1. This value k is further analyzed in relation to its relationship with other graph parameters such as the degree of the graph, the minimum number of edges in a shortest path, the maximum number of edges in a shortest path, and the diameter of the graph. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) vary significantly across broad energy spectra, and long observational periods are needed to fully understand their behavior. However, traditional analysis approaches are often hindered by data inconsistencies and different observation lengths, which can affect the accuracy of conclusions drawn from them. In this study, a novel method is introduced that seamlessly connects data sets with distinct lengths, even across different observations, and provides a marked improvement in modeling variable AGNs. The approach utilizes a dynamic approach to handle data with varying lengths, which significantly enhances the performance of the damped random walk model by narrowing the 68% confidence interval and aligns with physical expectations from emissions and scattering processes. Furthermore, this study applies the developed technique to extensive datasets from the X-ray and optical spectra for the AGN VLTJ122435, revealing a significant increase in the confidence interval of its variability compared to previous findings. The resulting parameters also demonstrate that the damped random walk model needs to be modified further to accurately describe the variability of this AGN. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the advantages of a dynamic approach in analyzing long-term AGN variability and highlights the need for a more sophisticated model that captures the behaviors observed in VLTJ122435. The developed method and model are now available for public use on GitHub. The current study adds to the understanding of VLTJ122435, a super Eddington radio-quite AGN with variable spectra, and contributes to the broader knowledge of its behavior. In the context of multi-agent decision-making, establishing meaningful valuation functions for agents is crucial, as it can significantly influence the accuracy of algorithms aimed at optimizing overall efficiency, given limited information about individual preferences. Our study examines the resilience of approximate algorithms in a scenario where agents' true valuations result from bipartite matching or directed graph properties, which can be estimated with an error of at least a fraction of $1/e$ (achieved through an example based on a well-known SDP relaxation). We demonstrate that for various combinatorial optimization tasks, including matching, vertex cover, and spanning tree, no valuation-based algorithm can achieve an approximation better than $1/n$ (where $n$ denotes the number of agents) even when valuations are relatively fair, as indicated by the absence of a gap between the upper and lower approximation bounds. To address this limitation, we propose a new algorithm that leverages fair valuations to enhance the approximation quality to a satisfactory extent, specifically achieving improved approximation ratios for the matching, vertex cover, and spanning tree problems. We also introduce a more general valuation-based framework that incorporates fair valuations, leading to a range of applications, particularly in scenarios involving inter-agent divisions of goods, where agents' true valuations arise from a specific type of graph property which can be inaccurate with respect to a fraction of $1/e$. We demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithm through comprehensive simulations covering various combinatorial optimization tasks and scenarios with divided goods, showing that it consistently matches the performance of its optimal counterpart in terms of overall efficiency. Our approach is valued for its simplicity, as it requires significantly less information about individual preferences during decision-making, although it is not universally applicable, as shown by examples based on random utility theory and preference elicitation risks. Our contributions are particularly relevant to large-scale decision-making scenarios, as they help establish robust valuation functions that can be used with efficient algorithm designs, leading to a range of applications in good division, group selection, and cooperative DSE. Our approach also involves a valuation-based extension of a well-known core concept, offering a more general and versatile framework that can be utilized in good division and group selection scenarios. Our findings address the limitation of prior research on valuations-based algorithms by providing a more rigorous analysis of approximation bound gaps, through the introduction of a new algorithm that enhances approximation quality, and a valuation-based extension of a well-known core concept, offering insights into combinatorial optimization tasks, as well as providing a robust valuation framework applicable to good division and group selection scenarios. To analyze network peer effects, researchers often utilize exogenous changes to explicit connections within a network. However, many networks lack clear edges, making it challenging to identify which changes constitute a meaningful peer effect. A common approach involves utilizing geographical proximity to substitute for explicit connections, but this method assumes that geographical peers have a similar impact on individuals from varying backgrounds. A more flexible approach is presented in this research that utilizes multiple peers from diverse origins to estimate unique peer effects and combines them with conventional methods that involve explicit connections to network peers. The accuracy of this approach is demonstrated using an empirical example--military recruitment in the United States--which exhibits complex network characteristics involving multiple peer groups. The results show that the effect of peer groups varies significantly, and failing to account for these differences leads to incorrect inferences about peer effects. Furthermore, the research provides guidelines on how to interpret peer effects on individual behavior that are specific to particular networks. A key application of this research is the analysis of social influence within military networks, which can, in turn, influence recruitment patterns. By incorporating peer effects from diverse backgrounds, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the complex social networks that shape individual decisions. Our in-depth analysis of four "superLooper"-containing proteins with a knot type known as the $3.1_{\gamma}$ knot reveals their complex folding processes. These deep knots require a distinct folding mechanism, unlike the simpler knotted proteins that often follow the same folding path as their non-knotted counterparts, typically involving the formation of loose loops along the way. Through molecular dynamics simulations and by comparing them to previous studies on two other deeply knotted proteins, we found that these proteins avoid loop loop interactions that could lead to misfolding, instead adopting a more precise approach that ensures the correct pairing of segments throughout the folding process. This precision is made possible by the unique properties of the $3.1_{\gamma}$ knot design, where specific segment interactions are necessary to maintain stability, thus ensuring that any temporary loop formations are necessarily productive, leading to a more direct path to achieving the final knotted, folded state. Our studies highlight the significance of loop loop interactions in the folding process of these deeply knotted proteins, offering valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying their folding processes. Our proposed superLooper classification provides a meaningful distinction within the protein knot family, while our findings also address the broader question of how protein evolution accommodates the formation of knotted structures that demand greater precision in folding processes. The Nambu-Goldstone theorem is inherently linked to the spontaneous breaking of continuous symmetries in physics. However, the generation of mass in massive Nambu-Goldstone bosons remains a nuanced topic. The kaon condensation model serves as an intriguing example to analyze this phenomenon. In this paper, we delve into the concept of mass generation in the context of this model by incorporating the kaon condensate as a degree of freedom in the QCD Lagrangian. We then utilize the in-medium relation between the energy and momentum of kaons to compute the mass of massive NG bosons. A comparison with theoretical and experimental data reveals good agreement, with the mass of the kaon also being sensitive to temperature and density factors. Our analysis highlights the distinction between the mass generation mechanisms of the kaon condensation model and the usual massive NG bosons resulting from symmetry breaking. Furthermore, we discuss the applicability of this model to the sigma term problem in QCD. A calculation of the sigma term in the kaon condensation model at finite temperature and density is also presented. Our study suggests that the sigma term primarily depends on the density rather than the temperature, a finding consistent with earlier research. Our work in this paper has been previously published in individual studies, but this compilation provides a cohesive understanding of the complex phenomena involved in the mass generation of massive Nambu-Goldstone bosons within the kaon condensation model. Despite the complexities, our results demonstrate the feasibility of describing the mass generation of massive NG bosons using the kaon condensation model, with the mass being distinct from the mass generated by symmetry breaking. Consequently, this demonstrates that massive NG bosons can arise in scenarios beyond the usual quadratic potential, where the mass is directly related to the vacuum expectation value. While the MAD model effectively explains lower energy gamma-ray data, it falls short of fully accounting for higher energy data, particularly those gathered by the Fermi Satellite. This remaining unexplained portion of higher energy gamma-ray data is quite substantial, exceeding $10^{-3}$ when considering collisions involving protons and is especially prominent when considering collisions involving heavy particles like lead. This remaining unexplained portion of data could be the result of particle collisions that produce gamma-rays through other mechanisms, such as the Bethe-Heisenberg process, in addition to the usual quark-gluon collisions. Furthermore, this unexplained portion of data may also be affected by certain issues related to the geometry of the detector used to gather the data. The proposed structure ensures the consistency of the anisotropic diffusion process, resulting in a consistent anisotropic minimization problem. The proposed method exhibits promising performance, outperforming conventional methods, especially in noisy data sets, e.g., with background noise. This approach has the advantage of being universally applicable to other medical image analysis tasks involving non-regular shapes. Medical research institutions and organizations are increasingly using federated learning to tackle challenges in predicting patient outcomes and identifying wearable activities. Despite its potential, educating the population to accurately identify physical activities from wearable data remains difficult, as input data privacy concerns force institutions to retain control over their data. This issue prompts a investigation into methods of educating the population about patient outcomes and activity recognition without accessing private data. To address this problem, an innovative approach called FedHealth was developed to enhance the accuracy of activity recognition on wearable devices by securely sharing encrypted data between institutions and the population. In evaluating FedHealth through synthetic data generation and real-world examples, significant improvements were observed in predicting activity types and whole-body movement levels. Furthermore, by scaling FedHealth to a larger user base, researchers discovered that incorporating data from 10 users provides a 3.5-fold increase in performance compared to 1 user. Ultimately, FedHealth offers a groundbreaking solution for accurately predicting patient outcomes and identifying physical activities from wearable devices without accessing private data. The limitations of FedHealth are discussed, along with potential future research directions, such as incorporating additional sensors, and developing a more advanced approach to handling data anomalies, in order to further enhance the effectiveness of this framework. The efficiency of an interview panel can be significantly enhanced by employing algorithms to assign candidates to open position interviews and create panels, thereby minimizing travel requirements for assessments. To tackle this challenge, we develop two distinct solutions. Firstly, we introduce a mark-sense algorithm to determine the scores of candidates after interviews, thereby enabling panels to be established for assessment interviews. Here, each panel consists of interviewers assigned to evaluate specific aspects of a candidate. We prove that the proposed algorithm yields optimal panel configurations, achieving the lowest possible sum of distances for each candidate. Secondly, we devise a consecutive tour algorithm to create panels for face-to-face interviews with multiple assessors. This algorithm ensures that candidates are assigned to tours where assessors are arranged in an order that minimizes the total distance traveled. Both algorithms are tested using real-world datasets and produce results that surpass existing solutions. Additionally, they provide optimal combinations of panels for each candidate, enabling easy comparison of assessment outcomes. In general, employing algorithmic approaches to panel creation and assessment interviews can lead to a significant reduction in travel costs and assessors' time, while also facilitating fair assessment processes. In recruitment processes involving multiple assessments, algorithmic panels can result in up to $10^8$ times faster computation and more accurate outcomes than traditional methods, depending on specific application scenarios. Experimentation with real-world datasets reveals that algorithmic panels can yield assessments that are $20-40$ times more accurate than those produced by traditional methods, as measured by agreement among assessors. In cases where assessment scores are initially available, the algorithm can further enhance the accuracy of outcomes by up to $10$ times, indicating that algorithmic panels can be highly beneficial for a broad range of recruitment processes involving face-to-face assessments with multiple assessors. In situations where travel distances between assessors and candidates are unknown, we propose a simple and efficient algorithm to determine the most cost-effective combinations of panels for each candidate, thereby minimizing the total cost of travel required for assessments. This algorithm produces outcomes that are at most $4$ times worse than optimal solutions, while also providing feasible combinations of panels for each candidate that can be easily compared to ensure fairness in assessment processes. Notably, the algorithm is significantly more efficient than existing solutions, requiring up to $10^7$ times less computation to produce outcomes for large-scale recruitment processes involving multiple assessments. This project focuses on developing a method for fitting differential equations to data, which is relevant to the spread of diseases and other similar phenomena. Although a common approach exists for solving this problem, issues arise when using the method on large datasets due to the complexity of the model. To address this challenge, we explore a way to break down the model into more manageable parts and use a technique called numerical integration to solve one of the parts. This solution relies on the method we're developing being a type of Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, which it is not commonly associated with in the context of epidemiology. To make the model more biologically plausible, we add a feature that allows the spread of a disease to slow down as more time passes. We also establish the uniqueness of a solution to the equation when the spread of the disease can be reversed. Furthermore, we prove the optimality of a particular solution to the equation, which involves the spread of a disease through two populations that can affect each other in a specific way. We also show that this particular solution is unique when the spread of the disease can be reversed. To validate our method, we used a simulated dataset that we created ourselves and compared the results to ones obtained using the existing approach. We also used a different dataset that was collected from real-world data and the results showed that our method and the existing approach produced similar, acceptable results. However, our method used significantly less memory than the existing approach when using the real-world dataset. We also used our method to add some biological feasibility to a model that had been previously validated using the existing approach but produced different results when used with the real-world dataset. Therefore, we recommend using our method when considering the biological feasibility of a model but also using the existing approach for comparison purposes. A key challenge in DNA data storage systems involves managing storage partitions, as they require for repeated use. To address this issue, a system that reuses old codewords by correcting sequential errors can be utilized. The approach presented in this paper offers a novel method of encoding, utilizing two sets of identifiers - 'hot' and 'cold' - to differentiate between frequently and infrequently accessed parts, respectively. A specially designed pair of primers is assigned to each storage partition, with 'hot' codewords utilizing a specific pair, and 'cold' codewords using a second, more precise pair to enhance encoding accuracy. As a result, this approach enables efficient retrieval of 'hot' codewords and recovers 'cold' codewords through a process called 'thermocycling', thereby reducing storage costs and enhancing data accessibility over time. To demonstrate the viability of this approach, the authors conducted an experiment utilizing a 1 byte data set and a 460 million dollars price threshold, which led to a usable storage capacity of 33.9 terabytes. The results showed that this approach could reduce storage costs by up to 50% and enhance encoding success rates by as much as 90% by carefully managing storage partitions through a process called 'thermocycling'. Furthermore, this approach has the added benefit of extending the lifespan of storage partitions due to repeated use, thereby reducing the need for new encodings and the associated costs. Accurate modeling of riverbed geometry is crucial for understanding and managing water flows, particularly during flooding events. Existing studies face limitations in accurately estimating bathymetry in rivers with high sediment discharge and meandering channels. This study presents a novel geostatistical method, termed the principal component geostatistical approach (PCGA), which enhances the traditional geostatistical method (TGA) by accounting for the mean flow field dynamics. Utilizing PCGA, the research team successfully reconstructed bathymetry with low misfit values in two challenging case studies, one with meandering channels and another with high sediment discharge. The results showed that PCGA outperformed TGA, with the PCGA achieving more accurate estimations of depth and width in both studies. Furthermore, PCGA demonstrated greater resilience to model noise, as evidenced by the riverbed profile analysis. The PCGA algorithm is a data-driven technique based on statistical principles, which enables its broad applicability to various geophysical settings. The method's effectiveness in river bathymetry estimation suggests that PCGA has considerable potential for enhancing the accuracy of bathymetry models in a wide range of scenarios. Moreover, this revised version has a more versatile application, as it can now effectively handle surfaces that are more genetically diverse. This research investigates the performance of the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) preconditioner in the context of a nested iterative solver for the algebraic equation resulting from the displacement formulation of the continuous Galerkin Natural Neumann boundary condition. We show that this space can be naturally compactified using the technique of stable MRCs, but we also find that this compactification is equivalent to a natural compactification generated by using stable extensive systems. We demonstrate a significant distinction between the geometric and Hodge-theoretic compactifications of the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_d(\Delta)$, as well as the individual component spaces $\mathcal{M}^{ext}_d(\Delta)$ and $\mathcal{M}^{sm}_d(\Delta)$, demonstrating that the latter contains components that are not part of the former. As an application, we establish the regularity of the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_d(\Delta)$ for $d \geq 3$. The rapid evolution of SARS-CoV-2 and changing healthcare guidelines pose significant challenges in allocating limited ICU resources effectively, particularly in the early stages of the pandemic.  A critical issue arises when deciding which patients to admit to limited ICU beds, as determining the overall ICU demand from a large number of patients is complex due to limited data availability, noisy reports, and varying reliability.  To address this challenge, a novel approach is proposed that employs a combination of mechanical intelligence and linear regression to analyze specific features associated with ICU admission, with the goal of predicting the probability of a patient requiring an ICU bed for the duration of their hospital stay.  This predicted value can be utilized to prioritize patient admissions and allocate resources more equitably.  In addition, feature analysis is provided that offers insights into the characteristics of patients who require ICU care and provides a framework for designing subsequent models, enabling seamless integration with existing healthcare practices.  A comprehensive evaluation of the model is conducted through a simulated example and real-world data from the ICU units of two hospitals in the United States, with results indicating that it is possible to accurately predict ICU demands from a large number of patients with limited data, leading to a proposed solution that can be applied to resource allocation decisions in various healthcare settings.  The model also demonstrates features that facilitate seamless integration into existing healthcare practices and prioritization schemes, as well as providing actionable data for healthcare providers.  Furthermore, the challenge of predicting ICU demands from a large number of patients is positioned as a critical example of a broader problem -- estimating uncertain quantities from unreliable and varied reports -- for which a mechanical intelligence-based solution is proposed and evaluated through the use of simulated and real-world data, before being compared to conventional machine learning techniques through the use of accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and mean squared error metrics.  The evaluation of the model also includes an analysis of its costs, reliability, and variability, as well as incorporating feedback from healthcare professionals to ensure its feasibility and validity in real-world healthcare settings.  The mechanical intelligence framework is further utilized to conduct a comparative evaluation of linear regression models with traditional and weighted variants, as well as nested models, through the use of a robust cross-validation technique that enables reliable estimates of model accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and mean squared error, as well as allowing for the detection of model overfitting and the identification of most informative reports.  The evaluation process is then generalized into a framework that can be applied to the assessment of other machine learning models and linear regression models in various healthcare

This connection leads to a characterization of the monad structure, thereby providing an alternative explanation for the properties it must possess. Furthermore, the paper establishes a connection between the universal bundle functor and the standard inner automorphism functor following Grothendieck's conception. This is achieved by constructing a natural transformation between the two functors, which induces the same monad structure. The paper also examines the relationship between the universal bundle functor and the standard inner automorphism functor in the context of simplicial presentations. Ultimately, it demonstrates that the universal bundle functor can be regarded as a right exact functor acting on the category of simplicial presentations, rather than simply being a functor within the category of simplicial groups. The paper presents a key result that originates from this understanding of the universal bundle functor, which has a significant implication for the category of simplicial presentations itself. The paper concludes by proposing an abstract framework of which the universal bundle functor is a part, presenting a general idea that the standard inner automorphism functor arises from it, and deriving a crucial property of the category of simplicial presentations. This paper investigates a one-dimensional transport equation with periodic conditions, where solutions can be expressed as integrals and the flux term involves a nonlocal operation, specifically the Hilbert transform. We consider an initial condition that starts from a smooth, odd function and shows that the solution will become unbounded in a finite amount of time if either the space period or the nonlocal integral coefficient is greater than 1. Furthermore, when both the space period and the coefficient are less than 1, we prove that the solution will eventually become infinite on the positive x-axis within a specified time frame. To obtain these results, we utilize the properties of the Hilbert transform along with the methods described by Panxiao Yuan, where we also draw upon the work described in Yuan's paper that demonstrates the solution's blow-up time can be determined in this specific case, and how it relates to the space period and the coefficient. Moreover, we observe that when the space period is greater than 1, the solution will experience blow-up at both ends of the space period, whereas when the coefficient is greater than 1, the solution will experience blow-up at the origin. This paper introduces a concept of power series in multiple variables that is useful in applying homotopy theory to problems involving partitions. A key element in addressing these problems involves graded polynomial rings, and we develop a comprehensive framework within which these rings can be combined to interpret partitions of a specific type. This framework, represented by a structured graded polynomial ring, serves as the underlying basis for a specific type of topological structured ring. We then establish a direct relationship between this ring and a specific type of Gamma-space, thereby providing a straightforward computational method for obtaining power series defined on the partition poset. This approach can be applied to evaluate the power series associated with the motivic exponential function on a given set, and we demonstrate how this evaluation leads to the motivic logarithm being representable as an element of the ring mentioned earlier. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when the base field is complex, this ring corresponds to a specific type of analytic structured ring, and we can determine the power series associated with the additive structure of the exponential function in this setting. This allows us to demonstrate that the power series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x_n}{n}$ has a finite radius of convergence within the context of homotopy theory. We also explore the connection between this convergence and the properties of the Gamma-function in number theory. Moreover, we establish that the structured ring mentioned earlier can be used to interpret the image of the motivic logarithm, thereby providing an alternative description of the ring defined by Deninger. We then discuss the relationship between the power series mentioned earlier and the negative part of Riemann zeta-function, and we demonstrate how the convergence of this power series can be used to interpret the value of the Riemann zeta-function at negative integers within the context of homotopy theory. This interpretation reveals that the values of the Riemann zeta-function at negative integers are the coefficients of the power series associated with the additive structure of the exponential function, and they are equal to the negative coefficients of this power series, thereby confirming the result conjectured by Langlands. We also establish that the structured ring mentioned earlier can be used to interpret the values of the Riemann zeta-function at negative integers within the context of homotopy theory, and this interpretation leads to the conclusion that these values have a finite radius of convergence, which provides a homotopy theoretical explanation for the finite nature of the radius of convergence observed in the number theory context. This explanation is independent of the characteristics of the base field.

Recent advances in natural language processing are largely driven by large language model pretraining, and our research strives to understand the fundamentals of this paradigm by examining one of its core assumptions: that models trained on factual knowledge triples outperform those trained on traditional text-based data for question-answering tasks. To investigate this assumption, we designed three standard question-answering datasets and found that models pre-trained on TPU-based knowledge graph triple storage lists performed better than those trained on BookCorpus. However, when we analyzed the underlying mechanisms behind this difference, several interesting patterns emerged, including the presence of noisy triples in knowledge graphs, inconsistencies in question types across existing datasets, and model performance fluctuations due to hyperparameter changes. To rectify these shortcomings, we created a new question-answering dataset called RuTQA, which is tailored specifically for testing models pre-trained using knowledge graphs and released it publicly for research purposes. On the benchmark datasets, RuTQA demonstrated superior performance when compared to existing datasets. When we removed noisy triples from the knowledge graphs, models pre-trained on triple storage lists performed significantly worse than those trained on text-based data, providing evidence for the presence of noisy triples and other suboptimal structures in knowledge graphs that can lead to model performance being below expectations. To address this issue, we proposed a simple multi-task training model that simultaneously answers questions from RuTQA and generates relevant triple verification, and as a result, model performance improved significantly. Furthermore, our research revealed that models pre-trained on triple storage lists performed poorly on questions requiring long context, which could be caused by the limited context range in the BERT model itself. To overcome this context limitation, we conducted multiple round training experiments on RuTQA and verified that models pre-trained on triple storage lists can handle a wider context range than those trained on text-based data, thereby supporting the feasibility of our approach. Our proposed model achieved notable success in various question-answering tasks, surpassing the performance of models pre-trained on text-based data by a significant margin of 10.3%. Our research is expected to provide valuable insights into the pretraining of language models using knowledge graphs, pave the way for developing more efficient model pretraining methods, and facilitate the widespread adoption of low-cost large-scale model training. A basic two-fluid model is proposed to describe an interface between a stable, slowly moving fluid and a highly turbulent, rapidly moving fluid in a cell with a heated bottom plate. By assuming that the interface lies parallel to the plate, the model successfully explains various observed phenomena of Rayleigh-B\'enard convection, especially the narrow range of the heat flux ratio for different interface speeds. According to the model, the heat flux through the interface follows a power law with respect to the interface speed, which agrees with experimental data. Furthermore, the model predicts that the heat flux is proportional to the square root of the temperature difference between the hot plate and the surrounding stable fluid, which has not been previously investigated in experimental studies. The model also offers insights into unusual patterns observed in the temperature fluctuations at the interface. The results presented here provide a framework for understanding the interfacial heat transfer in convection with a moving interface and offer potential applications to other similar systems, such as free surface flows with internal obstacles or composite materials, and serve as a starting point for improving the model by incorporating the effects of the curved interface and the resulting shear stresses. The simple model can be further improved by incorporating the effects of the curved interface and the resulting shear stresses, which could provide an even more accurate description of the heat transfer and fluid flow dynamics in these complex systems. The relationship between the interface speed and the heat flux flux ratio has been extensively explored in various experiments, but the underlying dynamics of the interface remains not well understood, filling the research need outlined in the question. The model's predictions have been validated in experiments with interface speeds ranging from 0.1 to 3 mm/s and height differences ranging from 7.5 cm to 1 m, and the limitations of the model have been tested with experimental data from other similar systems, such as free surface flows with internal obstacles or composite materials. A single cavity is connected to two channels, allowing for the exchange of photons with two atoms located in separate compartments. Initially, one atom is placed in each compartment, with the atom in the first compartment being unentangled and the atom in the second compartment being in a Bell state entangled with the cavity, while the cavity is also unentangled. This setup forms the basic structure for a classical two-qubit system and allows for the generation of four-qubit GHZ and W states through specific interactions between the cavity and the two atoms. However, due to cavity decay, there are limitations on using this system to create high-level multipartite entanglement among the atoms. Nonetheless, suitable parameter selection can delay the onset of over-saturation, thereby increasing the availability of suitable time windows for generating multipartite entanglement among the atoms. Given the intensity of public discussions on high-profile news, modeling social media sentiment can be challenging, especially when using short-text baselines. This study focuses on classifying Twitter sentiment using long short-term memory networks, and our results show that LSTM networks can effectively capture the structure and content of tweets with little additional features. As a result, we recommend using LSTMs for sentiment analysis of short texts and provide a concise code snippet for ease of use. As an example, we apply this method to the Multiservice Yelp dataset and achieve a 79.1% accuracy rate with no extra lexical features. Furthermore, we successfully classify the sentiment of 20,000 anonymous Twitter messages with an 83.8% accuracy rate using only bare minimum features. By utilizing the Wigner function representation, we observed intriguing nonclassical phenomena associated with entanglement dynamics, including the creation, manipulation, and destruction of entanglement caused by photon loss and passive unitary transformations. Our approach to examining optical tomograms reveals the intricate behaviors of complex systems, offering a comprehensive understanding of entanglement evolution, which could be valuable for developing practical strategies to maintain and manage entanglement in various optical setups. Our results, presented in a graphical format using Wigner function dynamics, have the potential to provide insights crucial for experimenting with real-world implementations of optical entanglement dynamics. Our work demonstrates that Wigner function optics provides a powerful tool for visualizing and analyzing the entanglement dynamics within Mach-Zehnder interferometers. We also propose an interpretation of the Wigner function's negative domain as the source of entanglement generation and manipulation, in addition to its conventional understanding related to quantum nonclassical behavior. We observe that all operations performed on the interferometer are reflected in its Wigner function, with photon number correlations specifically influencing the entanglement evolution. We propose that the Wigner function's framework can be applied to other optical systems, such as three- and four-wave interferometers, as well as generic dielectric structures, offering a versatile platform known as Wigner function optics. We also introduce the concept of plotting Wigner function evolution in a 3D format, known as the Sarfatti plot, which we find facilitates the identification of distinct features associated with both classical and nonclassical phenomena. Video subtitles contained within the viewing area can complement the visual information and steer viewers' expectations for upcoming video frames, particularly for immersive videos. This study proposes an integrated viewport prediction framework that utilizes a self-expectation mechanism and incorporates video subtitles, yielding superior viewport prediction accuracy when viewing immersive videos with accessible subtitles. This approach first employs a self-expectation mechanism to generate preliminary viewport predictions and subsequently integrates the features of video subtitles and the viewing area to produce a more precise viewport prediction. Experimental evaluations reveal that the proposed framework outperforms the baseline methods, demonstrating the significance of video subtitles in predicting viewers' expectations for upcoming video frames. This discovery is further supported by viewer experience surveys and subsequent video subtitle and viewing area modification experiments. Moreover, the proposed framework is found to be efficient in model parameter utilization and resembles conventional viewport prediction networks in terms of structural composition. This efficiency and structural simplicity are further highlighted through model efficiency comparisons and structural analysis, respectively. This research poses potential applications and challenges for improving viewport prediction accuracy through video subtitles and presents the framework as a viable solution for delivering immersive videos with accessible subtitles for viewers with disabilities. This is particularly crucial for the increasing number of viewers with disabilities and the expanding use of immersive videos in everyday life. This approach also offers insights into viewport prediction models and provides a tangible example of successful model utilization for auxiliary information in a new context. This is demonstrated through the comparison of model learning pathways for original and self-expectation viewport prediction tasks, revealing distinct learning patterns and pathways. This research is significant for the multimedia community, particularly within the spheres of immersive video viewer experience prediction, accessible videos, and the utilization of auxiliary information. This is reflected through the utilization of a publicly available code repository at the following link: https://github.com/ZhouYi1999/Viewport_Prediction_with_Subtitles. This research is further supported by viewer experience and video subtitle/area modification experiment surveys, alongside experimental evaluations and comparisons. This knowledge can be applied to enhance the viewer experience for immersive videos with accessible subtitles and disability-aware video design. This is shown through viewer experience and video subtitle/area modification experiment surveys, alongside the discussion of potential challenges, limitations, and future work in this field. The property achieved here improves upon previous results, obtaining a larger class of allowable external fields. Furthermore, the property obtained can be related to the dispersion of approximate periodic solutions, demonstrating its applicability to a broader context. A study on the impact of these effects on the gluon distribution, specifically in the $x$-dependence, has been conducted. The contribution of infrared renormalons to the gluon distribution's uncertainty is significant, with an estimated effect of $10^{-4}$ on the gluon distribution at a $p_T$ scale of 1 GeV, or $10^{-3}$ on the hadronic cross-section for top-quark pair production with a 14 TeV LHC. Knowledge distillation (KD) is a technique for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic a pre-trained high-capacity network. However, standard KD requires access to the expensive network's output, making it unsuitable for certain black-box settings. A new approach, decision-based black-box knowledge distillation (DB3), is introduced, where the compact model is trained to match the decision-making process of the pre-trained network, without using its output. In this approach, only the network's input and a target vector are required, where the target vector represents the network's desired classification for each training data point. An optimization algorithm for DB3 is also presented, along with theoretical proof showing that DB3 reduces the model's size while maintaining the original network's classification performance. Experimental validation across various network and data pairings demonstrates the effectiveness of DB3, revealing that it outperforms existing knowledge distillation methods in many cases. Additionally, an interesting finding reveals that DB3 can successfully train a model on a corrupted dataset, where the dataset's label noise is not known in advance. This leads to a new understanding of KD, showing that it is, in fact, a regression problem, where the target vector represents the network's desired classification for each data point, even in the presence of label noise. In such a case, a new algorithm is introduced that incorporates statistical techniques to estimate the target vector, resulting in better performance compared to standard KD in the presence of label noise. The proposed DB3 approach and algorithms are made available through the Knowledge Distillation Repository, an open-source platform for accelerating deep neural networks. This repository also presents additional knowledge distillation methods and algorithms, offering valuable resources for the community. Through rigorous evaluation and further experiments, it is demonstrated that the proposed DB3 methods are superior to existing knowledge distillation techniques, leading to the conclusion that decision-based black-box knowledge distillation is a promising technique for accelerating deep neural networks. This research is relevant to industries that utilize deep neural networks, including the one the authors belong to, which uses networks for various applications such as object detection, language models, and recommendation systems. A notable limitation of the research is the assumption that the pre-trained network's classification for each training data point is known in advance, which is not a realistic assumption in practice. However, this assumption is feasible in certain settings, such as when the pre-trained network is used to classify a fixed set of categories, where the desired classification for each data point is determined by the network itself. An analysis of $B$ meson decays into two neutral $K$ mesons is performed using 349 inverse femtobarns of LHCb data. This study evaluates the branching fractions for several decay modes involving neutral $K$ mesons, with measurements for $B^0\rightarrow K^0\bar K^0$ confirmed at the highest precision to date (at 0.44%) and findings for previously undiscovered decays like $B^0\rightarrow K^0K^0\pi^0$, $B^+\rightarrow K^0 K^0\bar{\nu}_l$, and $B^0\rightarrow J/\psi K^0\bar K^0$ made. Also examined is the $C$-parity violated process $B^0\rightarrow K^0 K^0$ with a lower limit on its branching fraction at 0.53% above the current record. This research yields updated estimates for the $B^0\rightarrow K^0\bar K^0$ process's phase factor, known as the mixing phase, and tightens constraints on the magnitude of the CKM matrix's smallest element |p| based on four-body decay analyses. Additionally, this compatible structure enables us to accurately reconstruct the lattice of submodules of M. This reconstruction approach can be applied to various modules, including those with nilpotent radical components, which we refer to as CCN modules. Notably, this module class includes the set of minimal simple modules for any solvable group G. Our research also explores the relationship between our reconstruction method and existing approaches, such as those used for groups with a soluble residual. Moreover, our results extend and modify previous constructions to accommodate distinct structural characteristics, ensuring that our reconstructed lattice modules retain their original underlying structures and share the same simplicity properties of the original modules. In the case of simple modules, our reconstructed modules correspond to the same irreducible representation of G. We demonstrate that our approach can be applied to a broader category of groups, including those with a soluble residual, by utilizing existing research on the subject. Our study on the subset of minimal simple modules M can be found in the paper "Structure of the Composition Factor Lattice of Minimal Simple Modules". We propose Co-Imitation Learning, a novel framework that enables agents to acquire expertise in multiple tasks by collaborating with a single mentor. In this approach, an agent and a separate imitator are jointly trained to mutually improve each other's behavior without requiring demonstration data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Co-Imitation Learning by applying it to two challenging scenarios: transferring policies in Reinforcement Learning and duplicating an agent's behavior in Multi-Agent Learning. Compared to existing imitation learning techniques that rely on expert demonstrations, our method has the advantage of leveraging policy-based inputs. Through comprehensive experiments, we show that Co-Imitation Learning surpasses conventional imitation learning methods and yields comparable performance to state-of-the-art transfer learning techniques. Furthermore, our approach is theoretically linked to both Adversarial Learning and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning. To facilitate broad applicability, we provide an open-source code for Co-Imitation Learning.

This research investigates how different bias values in the polarized cutoff rate affect a sequential decoder's performance. A biased cutoff rate was first introduced by Richardson and Urban, and it simplifies the problem by serving as a threshold for a sequential decoder. However, it can vary depending on the code and bias, making it an unreliable indicator of a code's error-resistance. To address this issue, we developed a method to calculate the minimum biased cutoff rate required to ensure a sequential decoder produces acceptable error rates. This approach involves establishing an upper limit for the biased cutoff rate and determining the minimum cutoff rate that satisfies this condition. To achieve this, we first establish the relationship between the biased cutoff rate and the maximum conditional entropy, then use it to find the minimum biased cutoff rate that meets the required standards. This approach applies to both fixed and variable-length polar codes. For these codes, we also established a lower bound for the minimum biased cutoff rate, and it reflects the code's error-resistance when used in a specific channel condition. This research provides the necessary framework for further optimization of the minimum biased cutoff rate, which can be refined with additional information about the code and required error rate. Ultimately, this research sets the foundation for developing more efficient and accurate methods to determine the minimum biased cutoff rate. This leads to more efficient and error-resistant polar codes, especially for applications that require tight control over the trade-off between code length and error rate. This research demonstrates its benefits in two such applications. The first application involves transmitting a long message in a cable, where the code length and error rate must be precisely controlled to avoid disrupting the transmission process. The second application involves emergency broadcasting systems that require efficient and error-resistant communication protocols to reach as many recipients as possible with limited code length and strict error rate standards. In both cases, the research shows that our approach can significantly reduce code length, thus allowing for more efficient and reliable communication. The testing method described in this research is also novel. Normally, the performance of a code is evaluated by testing it on a specific channel with a fixed bias, but our research proposes a more flexible approach that involves testing the code on various channels with different bias values, thus providing a more comprehensive understanding of the code's error-resistance in different scenarios. This research also introduces a testing environment that can be used to investigate the relationship between the polarized cutoff rate and conditional entropy, which has been little explored in the past. The results show that by optimizing the action prediction objective in addition to the standard policy optimization objective, the learning efficiency can be improved, and the performance of the model can be enhanced significantly even without any additional data. This research paper provides new operator formulations for recurrent operators and applies these formulations to evaluate the condition for biharmonic hypersurfaces to be minimal within Euclidean space. By utilizing these formulations, equations for Laplace-Beltrami operators and second order mean curvature operators are derived, and it is demonstrated that in order for a hypersurface to be considered minimal, these operators must both be equal to zero. Moreover, necessary and sufficient conditions for a hypersurface to be minimal are also obtained and proven. Finally, essential cases of plane and spherical cones are examined and shown to satisfy the condition of being minimal, whereas no other conjugate minimal hypersurfaces exist within Euclidean space. This is because the vanishing theorem of harmonic maps implies that beyond plane and spherical cones, no other conjugate minimal hypersurfaces exist within Euclidean space. This result can be viewed as a continuation of previous research on the minimalness of certain biharmonic surfaces presented in the paper "The minimalness of certain biharmonic surfaces" published in the journal Advances in Mathematical Physics, 2015. This study delves into the snapshot isolation theories for NoSQL databases, focusing on MongoDB's deployment of WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER. To understand the underlying behaviors of these deployments, we break down their mechanisms into individual components, then analyze the resulting behaviors using a theoretical framework of multi-version concurrency control. Our findings reveal variations of snapshot isolation that these deployments adhere to, as well as possible violations of consistency theory. Furthermore, we identify potential bottlenecks in their implementations. Lastly, our research suggests possible enhancements to ensure stricter snapshot isolation standards. Our code and research are openly available on GitHub, inviting feedback from the community. Recent studies near the Sun have revealed the energetic requirements for solar particles to reach certain distances, particularly within the inner heliosphere. In this work, we examine the energy distributions of solar protons with energies between 0.5-12 MeV, focusing on how these distributions change with heliocentric distance, specifically at distances of 0.48 to 1 AU, as observed by the Solar Wind Solar Observation (SWO) instrument on the Solar and Helios Optical Selection (SOHO) spacecraft. Our analysis shows that the most probable energy required to reach 0.48 AU is 2.5-5.5 times greater than the energy needed to reach 1 AU, with an energy increase of 1.4 MeV per 0.01 AU change in distance. Additionally, we note that the shape of the energy distribution also changes with heliocentric distance, with the standard deviation of the distribution increasing by approximately 20% every 0.01 AU. Notably, our findings suggest that extremely high-energy solar protons can reach the Sun relatively easily, but the majority of particles require much greater energy to navigate the inner heliosphere. Our research provides crucial insights into the transport and acceleration mechanisms of solar particles in the inner heliosphere, with implications for understanding events like stellar solar bursts. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the significance of observing the inner heliosphere globally and simultaneously to better comprehend the complex interactions within this region. The energetic barriers faced by solar particles in the inner heliosphere also have implications for modeling extreme solar events and, by extension, events on other stars. The comprehensive data from the SWO instrument enable us to explore energy distributions at unprecedented levels of detail, with the 0.48 AU observation revealing a previously unreported 'high-energy tail' of solar protons that may reflect changes in solar wind interaction or suggest that solar particles can be accelerated within the inner heliosphere through different mechanisms than those proposed for larger heliospheric distances. The detailed energy distribution data from this analysis will be valuable for modeling energy transport and informing future missions dedicated to the inner heliosphere, such as the Solar and Helios Optical Selection (SOHO) upgrade, the Solar Wind Solar Observation 2 (SWO2) mission, and the Inner Heliosphere Imaging Magnetometer network. The discovery of the high-energy tail and the associated shift in energy distribution may also necessitate adjustments to current modeling parameters used for events like stellar solar bursts. The accuracy of this method is demonstrated through comparative studies, showing notable speed improvements (e.g. from 0.73 seconds to 0.25 seconds for a specific example) while maintaining high precision (e.g. 97.5% confidence level in $5\times 10^{-6}$ range). Ultimately, this research leads to a superior hedge cost calculation architecture that can be applied to various complex financial transactions and instruments. The associated code is available on a public repository, offering user-friendly GUI and API tools for easy integration into existing infrastructure, allowing other financial institutions to leverage this method for improved hedge cost management, paralleling the findings of previous studies on the importance of efficient risk management practices. A generational equity framework is proposed to evaluate the distribution of chances in a society, enabling comparison across different populations of age. This approach asks two primary questions: How do opportunities for current generations affect future generations of the same age? How do opportunities for current generations of a specific age affect those of the same age in future generations? These inquiries are then applied to three cases studies: data on social mobility in the US, higher education funding in Germany, and higher apprenticeships in Germany. The results show that opportunities for younger generations are generally better than those of older generations in the same society. However, there are exceptions, such as the fact that younger US generations have lower levels of social mobility than older generations, and younger German generations have lower chances of completing their education than older generations, despite receiving more educational funding. The proposed method can be utilized to assess the impact of policy changes on future generations by considering factors like age, and it offers a useful tool for identifying age-specific effects on opportunities that are often hidden in other analyses. The research on German education systems also reveals that the differences in opportunities among different ages persist even after accounting for factors like income, education, and employment. The findings have implications for the design of policies aimed at improving opportunities for future generations, such as those benefiting younger generations at the expense of older ones, which may not be equitable in the short term but could be more equitable in the long term. The proposed method can be a valuable instrument for policy makers, researchers, and stakeholders evaluating the effectiveness of policies and programs intended for specific age groups within a society. In particle accelerators, the interaction between beams traveling in opposite directions causes them to shift from their intended paths. Researchers typically try to minimize this effect, but some of its consequences could be more significant than previously thought. Specifically, the beam-beam interaction can result in a consistent change in the radius of circular accelerators, a change that may be difficult to detect using conventional methods but could be found by closely examining the differences in the orbits of the beams after they interact. A calculation of the radial change caused by the beam-beam interaction has been developed and tested using data from two operating accelerators, demonstrating that this effect is real and may be significant enough to be seen in the behavior of particle beams even in large machines like the ones used in high-energy physics experiments. In such experiments, determining the properties of the Higgs boson relies heavily on understanding the behavior of these radial changes. Additionally, this effect could be useful for evaluating the performance of future accelerators that will likely have similar beam interactions. Ultimately, it may be necessary to revise the existing methods of evaluating the performance of these machines to accurately reflect the significance of this effect, which could provide a more precise basis for making physical and mathematical predictions about them. As for the two accelerators used in the research, the radial changes they caused resulted in a maximum deviation of about one ten-thousandth of the orbit radius, which is so small that it required the use of advanced statistical methods to detect it. These accelerators, known as the Large Hadron Collider and the ILC, are significantly different from each other in terms of their design, with the former being a much larger machine but one that moves at the same speed and includes the same type of beam-beam interaction. In contrast, the ILC is a more recent machine that moves faster and has a different type of beam-beam interaction but is similar in terms of the radius of the orbit radius. Consequently, the research was able to verify that the beam-beam interaction affects the radius of the orbit in the same way regardless of the machine design. Based on this discovery, it is likely that the effect will be significant enough to be seen in future accelerators that will likely have similar beam interactions. To prepare for this eventuality, it is necessary to revise the methods used to evaluate the performance of these machines, which will give a more accurate basis for making physical and mathematical predictions about them. These codes utilize a singular, complex tensor to correct up to $k$rasures (erasure of $k$ individual bits) and can accurately reconstruct the original data even when the input is partially deleted. A specific example of a gauge code is the "triple-trussia" code, which we have found to be an optimal solution for achieving stability in Z_2 classical condensed matter systems. This code can successfully correct the erasure of 2 bits from any given 3-bit triplet. In contrast, this paper argues that evaluating models' performance relative to their position in the process is crucial. To address this limitation, the paper presents a statistical framework for analyzing change in predicted outcomes as users move through the process. By measuring the difference in predicted outcomes before and after user interactions, the paper shows that this approach can help companies in two key areas. First, it enables companies to compare the performance of different prediction models by assessing the shift in predicted outcomes with each model. Second, the paper shows that by combining these models, companies can create a unified prediction model that accurately identifies high-value users. By applying this framework to data from a fantasy sports website, the paper demonstrates that this approach can effectively pinpoint high-value users with greater accuracy than traditional methods. As a result, companies can leverage this approach to enhance their revenue by focusing on the most valuable users. Furthermore, the paper provides an overview of the statistical framework and presents an illustrative example in the appendix. Additionally, the paper offers an R package called 'predictshift' that implements the proposed method, providing executives and data analysts with a practical tool to make data-driven decisions. Overall, the paper presents a meaningful extension to various machine learning extensions and offers companies a valuable solution to maximize their returns from prediction models by targeting the most valuable users. The study and associated package build upon previous research in areas like time-series forecasting, regression models, and customer relationship management. The paper is suitable for companies seeking to enhance their business processes and machine learning models, as well as academics interested in statistical analysis. Although this approach allows for a detailed investigation of the resonance's poles, the original paper lacks information on how the RPA framework relates the strength of the resonance to the strength parameter $\gamma$ in the four-body force interactions. To rectify this, we will re-examine the RPA formalism with a specific focus on this aspect and derive a new correlation that directly links the density of the four-body force poles to the strength parameter $\gamma$. This new understanding provides a clear connection between the RPA approach and the correlation classification of the four-body forces' poles, offering a more comprehensive understanding of this resonance's characteristics. Additionally, our study reveals that the strength of the four-body force interactions, as observed in experimental data, is relatively small, and this can be attributed to the four-body force's interaction density being restricted to specific neutron clusters. Consequently, the four-body force's impact on the giant resonance is limited, and this explains the larger resonance width when comparing RPA calculations to experimental data. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the depth of the four-body force strength parameter $\gamma$ could be approximately determined from the resonance width alone, based on the RPA calculation results and the established correlation between the density of the four-body force poles and the strength parameter $\gamma$. Notably, using this approach to approximate the strength parameter $\gamma$ yields a value of $-0.75 \pm 0.25$ MeV.fm$^4$, which is consistent with previous studies of the four-body force in $^{16}$O based on three-body force interactions. This shared value of $\gamma$ explains the observed resonance width width in $^{16}$O. This study explores the application of the Koopman operator framework to analyze nonlinear dynamical systems with localized observations. By utilizing a hierarchical learning model, we can extract global representations from localized data, facilitating the detection of hidden patterns and mechanisms. Although the Koopman operator can provide a global perspective, its observation of the system is restricted to a localized view, making it an 'embodied' observer. To fully utilize its capabilities, we must modify the learning model to account for its embedded nature, which we demonstrate through a numerical example using the Lagrange graph neural network architecture. The resulting model offers a concise, interpretable representation of the system's dynamics and can be applied to various domains, including physics, economics, and biology. Neural text generation performance can be enhanced by improving sentence representations. A novel approach called SparseGAN achieves this representation improvement by applying regularization to intermediate neural network layers while maintaining natural language processing fundamentals unchanged. Unlike common practice, SparseGAN's regularization is induced via convolutional neural network feedback, enabling the extraction of semantic features from dense representations. Successfully tested on seven datasets, SparseGAN demonstrates representation enhancement and significant performance gains in generated text quality, outperforming baseline models according to multiple assessment metrics. The code for SparseGAN is available on GitHub at https://github.com/SparseGAN/SparseGAN. As a bonus, a super-sparse variant of SparseGAN is provided, exhibiting reduced parameter counts without performance degradation. This approach can be integrated into existing neural text generation models to enhance their performance. As an example, combining SparseGAN with the Transformer model results in a more efficient and more effective text generation model. As a result, the SparseGAN framework proves invaluable for both efficient and effective neural text generation. Code availability: https://github.com/SparseGAN/SparseGAN. Prior code version availability: https://github.com/SparseGAN/SparseGAN/releases. Note: Due to the significant increase in model performance, it is recommended to use the sparse version of SparseGAN with a maximum of 50 million parameters to avoid overfitting. The sparse variant of SparseGAN can be configured to compete with large transformer-based models in tasks that require a large amount of context, such as conversational dialogue. This anchor's efficacy is demonstrated in two large-context generation tasks: summarization and conversational dialogue generation. To facilitate fair comparison, the code for evaluating generated short texts is also developed, utilizing the widely accepted reference-based metric LEAM, and is available at https://github.com/SparseGAN/LEAM-evaluator. A comprehensive examination of this concept involves assessing the viability of exchange, distribution of biological materials, and the preservation of life forms across the vast distances between stars. By examining these factors, we evaluate the ideal locations to search for life that could be transmitted through panspermia, focusing on the remnants of dying stars, binary and multiple star systems, and the surrounding molecular clouds. Accurate population density estimates are crucial in animal research, yet traditional methods can be expensive and time-consuming. Advances in acoustic sensor technology and modeling have led to innovative techniques like spatial capture-recapture models, which leverage individual animal encounters to estimate population sizes and densities without closed settings. However, these models require dense data, including detailed information about individual animal interactions, which can be challenging to obtain using acoustic data alone. Our study presents a method to enhance density estimates using secondary species as focal subjects by developing a multi-species SCR model that incorporates density estimates from secondary species, which tend to have more abundant data due to less rigorous capture requirements. We applied this model to data from songbird populations using recorded voices of cats as a secondary species, and it showed improved density estimates for these birds. Additionally, our model facilitated flexible density variation modeling by incorporating spatial information about vegetation types, which correlated with songbird density. Interestingly, our research revealed that density estimates for secondary species can be accurate even when they are not a significant part of the population, making this method a valuable tool for integrating secondary species into research about focal species. Overall, our multi-species SCR model offers a valuable tool for conducting cost-effective animal density research by capitalizing on the advantages of both dense data from focal species and abundant data from secondary species. This approach can be particularly beneficial for studying rare or hard-to-detect animal populations. Our work demonstrates the efficacy of this model using acoustic data, but it has broader applications for any research involving the integration of data from both dense and abundant populations. Our model code is available for use by the scientific community at https://github.com/USGS-R/Scram. Our study highlights the benefits of combining dense and abundant population data, facilitates cost-effective animal density research, and presents a valuable tool for studying rare or hard-to-detect animal populations.
