This enhanced framework enables us to define an operator derived from the compatibility condition, denoted as the Galois operator, which in turn allows us to identify distinct equivalent systems of differential modules. Furthermore, we can determine the relationship between the Galois operator and a specified operator that varies with a parameter, establishing that they are equivalent under certain conditions. Additionally, this framework facilitates an in-depth examination of the connection between the Galois operator and the monodromy operator, thereby yielding geometric and analytical interpretations. Notably, when the underlying system consists of a single differential module, the Galois operator is analogous to the monodromy operator, thereby yielding a precise definition of the monodromy operator even in the presence of parameterized systems. Moreover, we demonstrate that the Galois operator can be used to determine the relationship between distinct systems of differential modules, thereby establishing a natural connection between the monodromy operator and the Galois operator. Ultimately, this research provides a solid foundation for exploring the connection between the monodromy operator and the Galois operator within the context of differential modules. Moreover, it paves the way for examining the more general case of $D$-modules and looking into the deeper connections between the Galois operator, the monodromy operator, and the singularities of solutions to linear partial differential equations. In this process, we can derive meaningful results from the established framework, such as reconstructing the relationship between the monodromy operator and the Galois operator, as well as establishing the compatibility of the Galois operator with the connection operator, thereby facilitating a comprehensive examination of the underlying system. Testing environments are vital for ensuring software correctness by enabling automated error detection through tests. Although automated test results can pinpoint exact errors, determining corresponding code fragments causing these errors can be challenging, especially when existing examples are not sufficient to locate the error in question. To overcome this limitation, we present an approach that uses a subset of our automated test suite to identify the faulty code for a given failure test by repeating partial tests until it locates the erroneous code. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by incorporating it into our testing framework at Google, which yields a substantial decrease in effort required to fix errors found during testing of one of its software applications. Furthermore, our approach enables the addition of failure-specific preconditions to existing tests, leading to a significant improvement in test efficiency. Our findings highlight the benefits of automated code targeting in testing scenarios mentioned above and provide a practical solution for addressing the 'known unknowns' in software testing. Our approach and methodology are now part of Test4Talk, a publicly available testing framework developed at Google. We outline possible future enhancements to our approach, which it believes has broader applicability to the software testing community at large. We invite other researchers and practitioners to build upon this work by combining the advantages of automated testing and the underlying code it identifies. We demonstrate the automated code targeting approach on a subset of our applications at Google, which consist of highly scalable distributed systems, but we believe this methodology has a wider scope of application, including microservice-based systems and applications with similar structures. We emphasize that the algorithm itself is portable and can be adapted to various underlying testing frameworks. We propose code targeting as a distinct problem in the software testing lifecycle, separate from traditional testing, and provide an example of how it can be incorporated into existing regression testing techniques to accelerate the discovery of existing code changes prior to code review. Ultimately, we view code targeting as a means to enhance the effectiveness of automated testing through active learning, which we illustrate using test-driven development as an example. We also explore possible scenarios in which the target code remains unchanged despite repeated tests, and present possible solutions to address this challenge. We recognize the potential risk of over-fitting when repeating tests on a subset of the existing test suite, and suggest statistical methods to validate the efficacy of our approach on diverse sets of tests. Phi Delta is an association rules mining algorithm that generates all possible rules from a dataset, and these rules are ranked by significance. The algorithm's efficiency scales to large datasets, making it suitable for applications in real-world scenarios. Type A and D root systems provide mathematical frameworks, and by integrating them with the Phi Delta algorithm, we can create an innovative method for ranking and generating rules that are situated at maximal eigenvalues. This results in a distinctive feature that distinguishes our approach from conventional approaches using machine learning, which often lead to optimal solutions but do not guarantee a clear understanding of the underlying dynamics. By utilizing the phi function from the root system, we can establish boundaries for which rules are considered significant and excellent, offering a, previously unexplored, perspective on the concept of significance. Furthermore, our proposal presents an innovative solution for solving the significant rule generation problem, which is known to be an NP-hard problem, by incorporating the phi function as an additional constraint. This results in a specific set of rules that are considered exceptional in a given dataset. Ultimately, our proposal presents a novel, universally applicable methodology that is unbiased and unparametrized, making it a versatile solution for addressing various problems related to the generation of significant rules. This is demonstrated through the analysis of a real-world dataset relating to financial transactions. The resulting rules generated through this approach exhibit a notable match rate with subsequent transactions, indicating its effectiveness. We introduce a novel randomized distributed algorithm aimed at estimating the size of a specific type of network - specifically, networks composed of connected components with a single central component - using limited messages. Our algorithm executes on these networks without knowledge of their structure and requires only that the largest component contains O(d^2) nodes, where d represents the maximum degree of the network. Our algorithm achieves this size estimation task while utilizing O(log n) messages on average, where n represents the total number of nodes in the largest component. Our solution builds upon our previous published algorithm, and we derive this new application through the use of our new algorithm as a submodule within a larger distributed function computation task. Additionally, our algorithm exhibits appealing scalability properties, particularly when compared to non-distributed estimates obtained through counting techniques based on random walks, especially given the need for only limited messages. Our algorithm has been designed with an additional feature that allows it to accurately identify the largest central component in networks that consist of multiple such components, making it a more general solution. We also establish the scalability conditions under which our algorithm ensures the accurate estimation of the largest component's size. Furthermore, our algorithm extends beyond size estimation, as it can be modified to count interesting network properties, such as the number of nodes within the largest central component. Our approach is considered efficient due to the minimal message requirements, making it suitable for implementation on large-scale dynamic networks. Our algorithm has been rigorously tested through extensive simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness across various network scenarios. We analyze the performance of a novel nonparametric approach to queuing length estimation at intersections based on traffic flow data. A key aspect of this method is its simplicity, as it doesn't require any assumptions about the distribution of arrivals or queue behavior. Our study compares this nonparametric method to two common parametric approaches – the single-server queue and the MAP queue – using simulated data for various scenarios. Our findings show that the nonparametric method consistently matches the accuracy of its parametric counterparts, often surpassing their accuracy in many cases. Additionally, we found that this method accurately estimates queue lengths during peak periods, particularly when vehicles arrive independently, and it also performs well when short periods of high concurrency occur, as long as those periods are sufficiently long to be considered part of the intersection's steady-state queue behavior. Our research indicates that this nonparametric method is a more reliable option for estimating queuing lengths than traditional parametric methods. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the accuracy of all methods improves with increased concurrency, as well as in scenarios with longer queue timeouts and timeout intervals. Our study also highlights the robustness of the nonparametric method, suggesting that its accuracy increases significantly, becoming nearly unaffected by concurrency scenarios, whereas the parametric methods' accuracy in such situations remains relatively stable before converging to the actual queue length. Our findings provide compelling evidence for the effectiveness and versatility of the nonparametric method, highlighting the potential risks and limitations of using traditional parametric models to estimate queuing lengths based on traffic flow data. Our approach can be applied to real-world datasets, as demonstrated by our application of it to a large dataset from the city of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Our proposed method is valuable for its ease of implementation, as it does not require any prior knowledge of the traffic queue's behavioral parameters. We have made the code for this method publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/SeanSinger/NonparametricQueueLengthEstimation. Our study has implications for the assessment of intelligent transportation systems and mobility management platforms, highlighting the significance of carefully evaluating queue length estimation methodologies and selecting the most accurate ones based on the characteristics of individual locations and transportation networks. Our findings also highlight the significant advantages of nonparametric methods over traditional parametric approaches in this context. We introduce a novel solution to the Hamiltonian constraint in general relativity, also known as the 3+1 conformal formulation. In this approach, the constraint is transformed into a series of nonlinear, second-order partial differential equations for the conformal factor, which can be resolved through a non-upwind, primitive continuous scheme. Unlike conventional methods, this technique eschews the assignment of weights for the formation of the conformal factor, instead utilizing a different method that ensures the preservation of the non-upwind property and guarantees the satisfaction of the fundamental properties of the metric. Additionally, this strategy ensures that the (0,2) conformally flat metric can be accurately captured, even in the presence of high-density singularities. A non-uniform, dynamic grid is employed to solve the system of partial differential equations, which includes the set of nonlinear equations, the Einstein field equations, and the evolution of matter. A selection of scenarios, including quadratic gravity and an oscillating mass source, are used to demonstrate the effectiveness of this new scheme, showing that it can successfully reproduce both the formation of scalar blackholes and the properties of quasi-periodic oscillations. A anomalous Nernst-Einstein relation exhibits an enhanced diffusion coefficient in materials experiencing structural changes. This phenomenon has been observed in antiferromagnetic antiperovskites, which display a transition from antiperovskite to perovskite structure under HeII pressure. To understand this behavior, researchers studied the thermal and electrical properties of Mn$_2$oxides, specifically Ba$_3$Mn$_2$O$_{7\pm\delta}$. By utilizing high-pressure techniques and low-temperature transport and thermal measurements, scientists found that the diffusion coefficient in Ba$_3$Mn$_2$O$_{7\pm\delta}$ increases significantly during the crystal structure transformation, and this effect becomes more pronounced at lower temperatures. Furthermore, the research revealed that the perovskite phase of Ba$_2$MnO$_5$ also exhibits this anomalous behavior, and this result is supported by theoretical models proposing that the Nernst-Einstein relation can be affected by the perovskite structure's rotational distortion. This discovery in Ba$_3$Mn$_2$O$_{7\pm\delta}$ provides a unique example of how diffusion can be enhanced in solid-state phase transitions, and it demonstrates that perovskite structures experiencing rotational distortions can display unusual diffusion properties. This research Demons that diffusion anomalies can be influenced by various strains on the perovskite crystal lattice. This finding opens up possibilities for discovering new materials that exhibit unusual diffusion behavior, which could be useful for developing future technology, and it also sheds light on the diffusion mechanisms occurring within perovskite structures. This research has been published in the 22nd July 2024 issue of Nature Physics. Within the framework of p-adic Hodge theory, it demonstrates that every reduced modulo p crystalline extension arises from a G.K. Artin-Scheier cocycle, thus extending Dawidkowski's result for fields of characteristic zero to fields of positive characteristic. Furthermore, fields of characteristic zero are included in the connection, allowing for the intersection of their corresponding collections of cocycles to be examined. Additionally, necessary and sufficient conditions are provided to determine whether two given cocycles, one from the collection associated with a field of characteristic zero and the other from the collection associated with a field of positive characteristic, are equivalent. This examination is made possible by analyzing the relationship between the collections of cocycles in fields of characteristic zero and positive characteristic through the parameter p. Consequently, this investigation paves the way for further study on the geometric and arithmetic properties of numbers defined by cocycles in the context of p-adic Hodge theory. Specifically, it creates a pathway for examining interesting properties, including potential applications to Deligne's conjecture, the minimal polynomial of Galois groups, and the arithmetic of modular forms. This research was inspired by the works of Serre, Thuet, and Le, as well as the results of Min, on the subject of G.K. Artin-Scheier cocycles and modular forms. This equivalence enables us to modify an existing proof to show that a closed surface in n-dimensional space with bounded mean curvature and mesoscale flatness is topologically equivalent to a sphere. Additionally, we clarify the relationship between this new concept and two other conditions on surface curvature: one leading to the topological equivalence of a sphere and another resulting in a surface being planar. Furthermore, we examine the requirements for a disk in n-dimensional space with bounded mean curvature to be mesoscale flat, leading to a calculation of the surface area of such a disk for certain values of n. A genetic algorithm can be utilized to optimize phantom damage locations near self-sensing carbon fiber reinforced polymers (CFRP) by selecting training data sets, ultimately enhancing the accuracy of damage detection. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, a genetic algorithm was applied to a limited set of data featuring 20 sensors and 100 units of length in a 300mm CFRP bar. The results showed that by optimizing the location of a single training anomaly, the accuracy of anomaly detection improved from 75% to 100%. Furthermore, a genetic algorithm was capable of identifying the most effective locations for adding self-sensing capability to a composite, as demonstrated by a 20% reduction in mean squared error when the algorithm was given freedom to place sensors along the length of the bar. Ultimately, this study proved that genetic algorithm can facilitate the development of self-sensing composites with improved damage detection capabilities by strategically placing sensors. The research presented in this paper has been previously published under the title ``Genetic Algorithm Training for Self-Sensing Composites to Enhance Damage Detection Accuracy'' at the 33rd International Conference on Testing, Evaluation and Validation. We introduce a progressive nature-inspired lottery-based mechanism for open systems, specifically applying it to the Lotka-Volterra model of predator-prey dynamics. This mechanism incorporates different intelligence types, such as 'naive', 'rational', and 'intelligent', into the decision-making processes of species, and it offers a simple and versatile model for exploring complex interactions. By leveraging a novel algorithm that efficiently finds the Nash Equilibrium, we gain insights into the implications of different intelligence levels on the coexistence or extinction of species. These findings are further illuminated through computational simulations and an analytical study of a sample case study. Our research reveals that 'rational' and 'intelligent' species exhibit a tendency to deplete their resources, leading to a spiral into extinction, whereas 'naive' species are more likely to thrive. In contrast, the coexistence of species is possible under specific conditions, such as the presence of additional species that serve as a 'carrying capacity'. Our results also demonstrate how the adoption of 'naive' intelligence by a small portion of a species' population can significantly reduce the threat of extinction. In the context of the Lotka-Volterra model, our research highlights the inapplicability of the Nash Equilibrium, highlighting a limitation of this equilibrium concept when applied to dynamic systems. Our research also sheds light on the challenges facing the deployment of intelligent species in dynamic environments, and it highlights the potential risks and unexpected consequences of introducing such species, including their eventual extinction. Our research toward understanding the interplay between intelligence and ecosystem dynamics serves as a foundation for exploring more complex systems and real-world applications. The muon g-2 experiment at J-Park has observed a $7\sigma$ discrepancy from standard model predictions, sparking a $20$ million dollar funding for a future electron muon phase space experiment in the United States. Inspired by this development, a concept for a future Chinese electron muon phase space experiment at the Beijing Spectrum Driver is presented. Utilizing a $3.6$ GeV storage ring, this experiment would have the ability to investigate exotic dark matter, axion-like particles, and other new physical phenomena that could explain the muon g-2 anomaly, in addition to providing precise measurements of muon and electron processes. With optimization for low-luminosity, this experiment would be capable of exploring a substantial parameter space not currently covered by other experiments, with results expected to be presented at future physics opportunities workshops. A initial design and potential for an upgraded storage ring are also discussed. The research presented here is supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the Ministry of Science and Technology of China. The project's expected cost is approximately $69$ million Chinese Yuan, with construction anticipated to commence in $2025$ and experimental data collection commencing in $2028$. This experiment is proposed to conduct experiments for five years, with the goal of publishing initial results in $2029$. The project also has the potential to contribute to other physics research, including the study of rare electron processes, electron collimation, and material science using a 3d imaging detector. The research and development of this experiment are expected to advance the field of particle accelerator technology, with potential applications in other energy and material research. A preliminary assessment suggests that this experiment could become a leading global experiment for the study of muon and electron phenomena. Accurate brain-computer interface (BCI) decoding relies on precise electrical mapping between neural signals and intended actions. Recently, high-resolution electrocortical recordings during surgery provide valuable training data, but whether they can effectively predict complex behaviors has not been well established. To address this question, researchers from the University of California recorded high-resolution electrocortical activity in individuals with epilepsy or tumor symptoms while they walked. The study demonstrated a high decoding accuracy of 93.8% for predicting walking functions based on a limited set of cortical signals, surpassing the results obtained with conventional electroencephalography. Furthermore, the study found that decoded gait patterns align with those from real-world observations, exhibiting a walk-rest structure marked by slower cortical signals during walking. The current study indicates the potential of ECoG-based BCIs in predicting complex behaviors and offers a feasible strategy for enhancing the accuracy of such predictors by incorporating the body's position. The research has implications for developing a brain-computer interface that can safely and effectively incorporate elements of the physical environment, such as the ability to predict and execute walking. The current study appears in the journal eLife. The study also sheds light on the relationship between the brain's cortical signals and the physical actions of walking, presenting a method for reversing the mapping process, or 'decodability', which can be applied to this specific action. The authors propose 'decodability' as a quantitative measure of the ease with which particular actions can be predicted from cortical signals, offering a promising assessment tool for surgical patients who have had ECoG recordings. The study's findings have significant implications for the development of effective BCIs in the future. These groups display a significant form of flexibility, as they can maintain a vast array of dynamic patterns across various metric domains. Building on the framework introduced by Bestvina and Fulman, we focus on the phenomenon where a separating subgraph consistently yields a well-defined, finite orbit in the metric space resulting from its action over time. This robust, time-independent pattern can be observed across various scalar products, including those induced by the word metric, the Cayley graph metric, and the Grushko metric. Many real-world systems, including cultural networks and mobile communication connections, evolve over time, making dynamic graph representation a growing interest. In scenarios where complete dataset information is limited, learning general representations from related graph categories can be beneficial. To address these challenges, we present DECENNT, a novel graph enrollment network that tackles two difficulties in graph representation: scale-neutral learning and category-enrollment for dynamic graphs. To achieve scale-neutral learning, DECENNT incorporates a self-supervised graph augmentation module that enhances representation invariance across different scales, and incorporates a multi-scale graph attention mechanism to facilitate information exchange between graphs of varying sizes. Additionally, DECENNT incorporates a category-enrollment mechanism to facilitate the learning of category-specific representations and the exchange of information between graphs within the same category, allowing for the enrollment of new graphs into learned categories. To evaluate DECENNT's performance, we introduce a new dataset consisting of 5 categories of dynamic graphs, each containing 10 instances, and demonstrate its superiority over existing methods through comparative studies on graph classification and link prediction tasks. Moreover, DECENNT's performance is shown to be compliant with a key challenge of scale-neutral learning, as validated by a downward-sloping regression analysis. With its innovative scale-neutral learning framework and attention mechanism, DECENNT achieves superior performance in representing and classifying complex dynamic graphs, making it a promising approach for its applications in real-world scenarios. From a technical standpoint, the code and dataset for this research are available at https://github.com/ChengLiUIDECENNT. From a cultural standpoint, based on the analysis of a dynamic graph representing the co-evolution of COVID-19-related tweet hashtags on Twitter, DECENNT's performance is demonstrated to be comparable to that of static graph-based methods and machine learning models, while offering the advantage of learning from smaller dataset scales. Furthermore, by enrolling new nodes into this dynamic graph, DECENNT successfully predicts the formation of emerging sub-communities consisting of Twitter users. Moreover, with the incorporation of a category-enrollment mechanism, DECENNT demonstrates its potential in modeling and analyzing complex dynamic graphs by providing a concise and intuitive representation of graph categories, as validated by comparative studies and scale-neutral learning analysis. While conventional neural networks excel in classifying differences between biological and non-biological movement, they require significant amounts of training data and advanced setups. This paper introduces an innovative approach that leverages spatial reasoning to create a robust model capable of distinguishing biological from non-biological movement without explicit labeling. By simplifying the model's architecture and eliminating the need for additional training data, it facilitates efficient application to novel image tasks. Experimentation reveals that this approach surpasses the performance of conventional methods in biological classification and detects movement in images with minimal pre-processing. Furthermore, the model's versatility is demonstrated by achieving the best results in comparison to existing methods on multiple standard benchmark datasets for biological classification, including INRIA Bird, CVC- Matteo, and VGG Bird. Additionally, it is shown that this approach can be applied to a broader context of "what is moving?" detection in images by achieving the lowest error rate among competing methods on the newly introduced Bird-All and Aircraft datasets. Experimental validation reveals that models over-rely on camera movement and animals in particular contexts. Nonetheless, the proposed approach demonstrates a significant improvement in detecting movement in images, particularly in scenarios featuring both biological and non-biological movement. Ultimately, this technique provides a tangible solution for the intricate problem of movement classification in biological contexts with minimal data requirements. We investigate the convergence properties of the Nested Neumann algorithm, which is an iterative method for solving linear systems arising from nested convex optimizations. We demonstrate the algorithm's convergence at a rate tied to the inception depth of the underlying graph, thereby extending a previous result that relied on a specific matrix format. To achieve this expanded result, we establish an inception depth measure as a lower bound for a particular order of matrix factorization, specifically the V-shaped stack format. Furthermore, we show that the Nested Neumann algorithm converges at a rate controlled by the inception depth of the stacked matrix, which represents a significant generalization of its previous form. This research is motivated by the study of the Nested Neumann algorithm's performance on specific graph-structured systems, particularly those defined by a stack format, which provides a precise framework for understanding the algorithm's behavior. This research is an extension of a previous study focused on the Nested Neumann algorithm and the V-shaped stack format. This research can be found as a part of the author's doctoral dissertation. Recent theories propose that quantum systems can identify whether they are in the Anderson isolated phase simply by analyzing the topological characteristics of their energy spectra. Although appealing, determining these topological properties can be challenging, especially when the disorder is extensive and the system lacks a genuine bulk region. In our research, we developed an approach to directly extract the topological features of deep quantum systems from their local measurements by utilizing the power of quantum approximate errors correction. Specifically, we crafted a quantum code whose structure is closely related to the topological characteristics of a quantum annealer, effectively serving as a detector that reveals the topological properties of the underlying Hamiltonian from local interactions. As a result, we demonstrated that the average of local coupling terms among the code's physical bits accurately represent the topological invariant of the underlying Hamiltonian, thereby validating the proposed approach. Furthermore, our research provided a potential classical simulation framework for quantum annealers, allowing for the recovery of the underlying Hamiltonian's topological characteristics from local measurements. Our study also offered possible strategies for implementing the proposed code generator on various quantum hardware platforms. In the Anderson isolation scenario, we demonstrated that the proposed code's quality is directly related to the duration of the quantum anneal process. By combining our approach with an existing classification method, we successfully detected the topological characteristics of highly disordered quantum systems generated by Anderson disorder. Consequently, our research demonstrated that the topological characteristics of deep quantum systems with strong noise can be safely retrieved from local measurements. Our results are essential for the practical application of quantum annealers in sampling the energy spectra of quantum systems with strong disorder. For policy learning using efficient value function estimates, selecting the optimal sample size for testing can be critical. This study examines how different test samples affect the reliability of efficient value function estimates, specifically focusing on the context of single-step policy learning. Our main finding reveals that with small test samples, efficient value function estimates are overly confident, leading to poor policy performance. Conversely, larger test samples yield more precise value function estimates, enabling the identification of optimal learning settings. Our research also provides a theoretical framework explaining the relationship between test sample size, value function estimate reliability, and policy performance. Furthermore, we propose a straightforward approach to determine the optimal test sample size, which is validated through experiments using both simple and complex scenarios. Our findings and proposed approach can be applied to various policy learning tasks involving value function estimation. Our code is available at this link https://github.com/Chenghao63/policy-learning-testing-samples. Our research contributes to the policy learning domain by highlighting the significance of test sample size selection and providing a usable framework for efficient value function estimation, key components in policy evaluation and learning. Our work also introduces a novel approach to allocate sample sizes for testing in policy evaluation, which can be utilized in settings beyond single-step policy learning. Our research analyzed the transverse momentum distributions of charged hadrons, specific types of charged particles, and protons, as well as the behavior of pions and kaons in relation to elliptic flow within collisions of heavy elements. By collaborating with the ALICE experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider, we gained access to data from collisions of Xeon-Xeon nuclei at a high energy level. Our study allowed us to measure particle distributions and elliptic flow patterns accurately, and further enabled us to identify patterns of particle production and to compare these results with computer-based theoretical models. Our detailed analysis covered several key findings, including an examination of expectations based on established theoretical models, the behavior of charged hadrons and specific types of charged particles, the patterns of produced particles moving in the same direction, the patterns of produced particles moving in opposite directions, and finally, an comparison of our results with previous similar experiments. Our accurate measurements confirmed previously observed patterns of particle production and also revealed additional information that will be valuable for improving current theoretical models. Our research also demonstrated that collisions of heavy elements at a high energy level primarily result in the interaction of two gluelike substances that make up the nuclei rather than the direct collision of the nuclei's core components. Our study has significant implications for our understanding of the properties of heavy element collisions and the behavior of subnuclear components within matter. Our most notable discovery was that charged hadron and specific type of charged particle distributions exhibit a slight deviation from expectations based on established theoretical models, while still confirming the patterns of particle production seen in lower energy experiments. Our research further revealed that the behavior of produced particles moving in the same direction and the patterns of produced particles moving in opposite directions primarily result from the collision of the gluelike substances rather than the direct collision of the nuclei's core components. Our study also showed that the behavior of pions, kaons, and protons exhibits some variation with the collision energy, but still follows the general patterns of particle production seen in lower energy experiments. Our research has significant value for the physical and technical communities worldwide by providing a comprehensive analysis of heavy element collisions at a high energy level, and further enabling the improvement of current theoretical models used to understand the behavior of subnuclear components within matter. Our study can be used as a foundation for future experiments and also presents opportunities for students and researchers to gain valuable experience and knowledge in physics and engineering. In large wireless communication networks, implementing power control algorithms can significantly reduce interference and improve signal quality. However, implementing some power control algorithms can be challenging, especially in highly dynamic networks. A recent study demonstrated the effectiveness of binary power control in a small network with fixed links, showing it can match the performance of optimal power control. This paper builds upon that work, exploring the feasibility and performance of binary power control in large, dynamic networks with multiple users and time-varying links. Using an optimal power control algorithm as a benchmark, the paper compares the performance of binary power control in various scenarios, including both single-user and multi-user networks. The results show that binary power control can perform similarly to optimal power control in many cases, often achieving similar throughput and packet drop rates. However, in networks with severe fluctuations in link quality, binary power control may experience poorer performance. A key contribution of this paper is the development of a novel binary power control algorithm called DYNAMIC-BC, which adapts to changing network conditions by dynamically switching power settings in response to feedback from the network. This algorithm is then compared to several other power control strategies, including a random baseline for reference. The findings suggest that DYNAMIC-BC generally outperforms this random baseline, often by a significant margin, and can also perform well in comparison to other more sophisticated algorithms, although there are some instances where it may struggle. The development of DYNAMIC-BC and the accompanying results arise from a comprehensive simulation of a multi-user network with time-varying links, which the paper describes in detail. The code for the paper is available publicly on GitHub, allowing for the replication of the results and further investigation into power control algorithms. The research on DYNAMIC-BC highlights its potential for use in real-world applications and provides a foundation for future work on power control in dynamic networks, as well as offering an example of open research code. We present an infinite series of mathematical expressions that can be equal to 7 raised to the power of any positive integer n, expressed as a ratio of two sums of powers of 2, specifically (2^a - 1) and (2^b - 1), where a and b are positive integers with a not equal to b. We also establish a lower bound for the fraction representing this series, utilizing its connection to the binary representation of n, and demonstrate that when n is an odd number, this fraction can be minimized in a certain binary expression and will always be at least 7^(log2(3)) or approximately 33.19. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between this fraction and another, similar expression involving prime numbers, p and q, where the product of these expressions equals a prime number, specifically 7, and present one solution to this equation, 3^2 + (2^a - 1)(2^b - 1) = 7^2. We also uncover another solution to this equation, - (2^a - 1)(2^b - 1) = 7^2 - 3^2, with a different choice of a and b, than the one mentioned above. Finally, we establish that given any positive integer k, there exists a value of n, which can be any even number greater than 4, such that the expression (2^a - 1)(2^b - 1) equals k times 7 raised to the power of n. We conclude by highlighting the limitations of our findings and potential areas for further study. We also demonstrate that when n is an extremely large number, the most basic way to express 7 raised to the power of n, as (2^{log_2(7^n)}), is not the most efficient representation for large n, but rather one that can be much larger, specifically 2^{log_2(7*n)} for n > 4. We hope this research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between prime numbers and powers of two. The analysis of complex information networks, particularly those comprising textual data, poses a significant analysis challenge. Current methods are often restricted by assumptions of conditional independence between hidden variables and network topology, which are not universally applicable. We introduce the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), a probabilistic model that bypasses such assumptions by utilizing a hierarchical structure of both documents and topics within information networks. We then test this model's efficacy on two real-world datasets--CiteSeer and PubMed--using a Bayesian learning approach and results show that HDTM exhibits superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods such as LTMR and BCTM in predicting textual attributes and navigating the hierarchical organization of topics. Furthermore, an empirical study on the importance of model hierarchy reveals that prioritizing hierarchy leads to a better understanding of the underlying structure and helps identify both valid and spurious relationships between categories of topics. We also observe that categories of topics are closely related to document categories and there is less overlap between distant topics, demonstrating the HDTM's capability to capture both micro and macro-level aspects of textual data. Ultimately, HDTM's hierarchical representation and Bayesian learning framework provide a robust framework for uncovering the complex underlying structure of textual data within information networks. We have publicly available code and datasets for reproducibility purposes. We also propose a new approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model-based Semantic Mapping (HDTM-SM), which leverages the hierarchical structure of topics to enhance the effectiveness of word embeddings in preserving both micro and macro-level semantic meanings. Empirical studies confirm that HDTM-SM yields superior performance compared to existing methods using widely used evaluation metrics such as NS, P-R, and AUC. We have made the code and datasets for this experiment publicly available as well. We hope that our models and experiments will contribute to the development of probabilistic models that incorporate hierarchy and help overcome the limitations of traditional statistical techniques in analyzing complex information networks. To overcome this limitation, we propose a modified quantum annealing algorithm that includes a brief classical re-annealing phase following quantum annealing, and successfully simulate the annealing process for both quantum and classical devices using just 1-2 orders of magnitude more resources than the actual experiment. With this model, we're able to study the annealing gap's dynamics and several relevant metrics for a prototype quantum annealer, and our research finds that the annealing gap's width varies significantly throughout the annealing process, offering valuable insights that can be utilized to optimize the annealing protocol. Our results also demonstrate the potential advantages of re-annealing, a previously unexplored quantum-classical hybrid annealing method. Using a suitable range of rare earth elements, the theoretical analysis accounts for rare earth spin orbits, lattice distortions, and appropriate phosphorus oxidation states. Important factors contributing to 4e-band formation are identified, including rare earth 4f-state interaction with nickel 3d states and nickel 3d-state localization. These theories result in a range of possible ground states, including anti-ferromagnetic and self-doped states, which can be realized by adjusting the rare earth element and nickel 3d-state localization. The findings suggest that self-doped distribution of holes could give rise to d-wave superconductivity, as seen in lanthanum nickelate. The findings also offer a theoretical basis for predicting and optimizing rare earth element and nickelate materials with magnetic and superconducting properties. The general methodology presented can be applied to the theoretical investigation of complex materials comprising multiple elements. Researchers studied a quantum compass model with a Heisenberg interaction to explore its ability to accurately estimate damping parameters and found that the (1)/N variance of the compass state decreases in proportion to (d)/N for both collective and individual damping processes.
As a system's size increases, the variance of its compass state will exhibit a pronounced growth, offering a practical example of a quantum system that can serve as a efficient instrument for measuring damping, specifically in large-scale settings.
Furthermore, variational estimates demonstrated that the compass state can efficiently determine both the damping strength and duration with high precision, with the number of required measurement steps increasing in proportion to the square of the system's size. 
Consequently, a scenario with both individual and collective damping processes can be distinguished using just a few qubits, whereas higher qubit counts are ideal for accurately estimating the duration of damping processes. 
Therefore, a quantum compass model exhibits the capacity to efficiently measure various damping processes, making it a promising candidate for use in metrological applications. 
Additionally, this research reveals that the compass state's ability to demonstrate (1)/N number variance holds true for any type of interaction, not just Heisenberg interaction, and provides a valuable theoretical framework that can be applied to other discrete driven damping processes. 
Ultimately, this study shows that the compass state's simplified preparation, coupled with its inherent benefits, can serve as a driving force behind the development of quantum instruments for measuring damping in complex systems and networks. 
Moreover, authors propose that the compass state's inherent relationship with (1)/N number variance could serve as an indicator of a system's complexity, with direct implications for understanding the interplay between compass state formation and damping processes. 
Finally, this research is relevant to various real-world scenarios, including the measurement of decoherence in superconducting qubits, spin qubits, and trapped ions. 
In the context of classical systems, it has implications for the study of damping in mechanical oscillators, such as crankshaft engines and pendulums, as well as population dynamics and food webs. 
In network theory, it could be applied to the study of damping processes within small-world and scale-free networks.

Distributed learning models that utilize data from multiple sources are increasingly popular, but often suffer from significant communication costs necessary to converge on a unified model. This issue is particularly pressing in modern large-scale learning applications, which frequently involve extensive networking expenses. Our research focuses on developing a decentralized learning framework for multiple participants with distinct datasets, where students are allowed to exchange limited information with each other, but only the teacher needs to possess the final learned model. We develop a general learning algorithm based on random walks, which enables students to reach an equilibrium where they have learned the desired model, and then map this equilibrium to the final model desired by the teacher. We prove that the resulting learning process is socially efficient and fair for all participants. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this efficient fleet learning framework can be applied to various specific settings, including congestion games, resource allocation, and electric grids, all while ensuring that the learned model accords with the teacher's preferences. Our experiments show that when the students and teacher have different preferences, the approach ensures a more favorable outcome for the teacher in comparison to conventional learning methods. Our approach has been tested in simulated environments and shown to provide meaningful results. Our code is available at this link https://github.com/hengg3/FleetLearning. Our research contributes to various applications and provides a foundation for learning from multi-modal and multi-language data. We propose an intuitive evaluation metric, Teacher-Student Similarity (TSS), to assess the similarity between the desired model and the actual learning outcomes, which can be up to 24% more similar when using our approach compared to conventional methods. We recommend our approach for situations where communication costs account for 20% or more of the total learning expenses. Our approach has been successfully applied in tasks such as distinguishing between real and generated text, identifying the language of text samples, and differentiating between male and female speakers. Many therapies, including cognitive behavioral therapy, have shown a positive impact in reducing future crimes among individuals with mental health issues, particularly those guilty of violent and sexual offenses.  Although mental health treatments have a general record of reducing future crimes, some criticisms exist regarding the current research methods.  These limitations include an insufficient consideration of treatment variations, to precise measurements of the same phenomena, and inadequate consideration of the timing of future crimes.  This paper used proprietary data from the National Offender Management Service (NOMS) in the UK to evaluate the effect of cognitive behavioral therapy on future sex crimes among offenders in the community.  It also compared the outcomes of different cognitive behavioral therapy programs.  Furthermore, it examined the exact timing of future sex crimes committed by offenders in the community.  The primary data consisted of around 5000 starting points for 8000 separate future sex crimes committed by approximately 1500 different offenders who received cognitive behavioral therapy as part of their sentence.  The secondary data included results from around 12000 starting points for 24000 separate future sex crimes among 2400 different offenders with similar characteristics but without cognitive behavioral therapy.  Both sets of data allowed for a precise measurement of the time it takes for an offender to commit another future sex crime after leaving prison, as well as the proportion of offenders who commit future sex crimes within a specific time frame.  The findings showed that cognitive behavioral therapy reduces the number of future sex crimes among offenders in the community by two-thirds.  It also cuts the time it takes for an offender to commit another future sex crime after leaving prison by half.  Finally, it lowers the proportion of offenders who commit future sex crimes among the community by two-fifths.  Additionally, the research discovered that the effect of cognitive behavioral therapy remains unchanged even after considering factors such as the length of prison sentences, the severity of crimes, and previous convictions.  It also found that the West Midlands had the highest number of future sex crimes among offenders in the community in comparison to other regions in England and Wales.  It was, however, lower in areas with higher levels of social deprivation.  The most significant future sex crimes among offenders in the community were committed exactly one year after leaving prison, and the most common offenders who committed future sex crimes had committed crimes such as gross indecency and flouting local restrictions. The main purpose of this paper is to demonstrate how the weak convergence of sequential estimates can be applied to achieve functional estimates of parameters. We establish the weak convergence of the sequential estimates used to reach a performance metric at a given threshold, which enables us to determine functional quantities such as the optimal threshold and the corresponding optimal performance metric. These functional quantities are treated as unknown parameters, and we develop sequential estimates for them. We then combine these with optimal scaling algorithms to obtain strong performance metrics. The weak convergence of the sequential estimates is established using the regularity condition, and functional quantities are estimated by treating them as fixed parameters. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to the optimal threshold and performance metric for detecting a change in the mean of a Poisson count process. The design of the sequential scheme is connected to maximizing the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and we derive the optimal scaling algorithms for this purpose. The results show that our approach successfully estimates the optimal threshold and the corresponding AUROC, and these are closely related to the optimal scaling algorithms. The auROC is found to be highly correlated with the sum of the sequential estimates, and we suggest alternative performance metrics that are easier to estimate. The challenge of implementing sequential schemes that maximize AUROC is addressed by providing a data-driven method, and the auxiliary algorithms are made publicly available as an R package called 'facs'. The performance of 'facs' is evaluated using a set of simulated scenarios, and the limitations of using the sum of the sequential estimates as a performance metric are discussed. The implications of our approach for changing the performance metric in detection problems are broad and can be applied to other processes and algorithms. The R package 'facs' can be downloaded from CRAN, and the code to generate the simulated examples is available in the package 'facsextras' on GitHub. Deep learning knowledge tracing evaluation methods are diverse and often require a vast amount of data to tune their parameters, which can be challenging to accomplish with limited anonymous clicks data. To address this challenge, our team proposes a new approach called Deep Knowledge Tracing Few-Shot Learning (DKTFSL), which leverages reverse knowledge tracing to generate suitable data for tuning deep learning models with only a small amount of anonymous clicks information. DKTFSF Learning utilizes an adversarial knowledge graph generator network to produce high-quality knowledge graphs, and combines them with noisy knowledge graphs from current LKT datasets through partial label matching to produce usable data for fine-tuning deep learning models. Our experiments conducted on three diverse LKT datasets show that DKTFSL achieves significant performance improvements over existing deep learning knowledge tracing models and standard recurrent neural network-based knowledge tracing models. Furthermore, our team demonstrated DKTFSL's effectiveness with multiple deep learning models, as well as various adversarial knowledge graph generator networks and model architectures to facilitate other research in the field. Our code has been made available open-source on GitHub.

Given a smooth function f belonging to the domain of the second-order elliptic differential operator H, the concept of surjectivity can be characterized by the existence of a function u, such that the equation Hu = f is satisfied. In this study, we establish that the set of surjective differential operators H corresponds to the presence of a continuous integral inequality involving the Carleson measure and the L^2 norm of f. As one of the study's key findings, we discover that the set of surjective differential operators H is nowhere dense within the context of smooth functions. Moreover, it is observed that for any given p > 1, the set of surjective differential operators H does not contain any functions belonging to the space C^0(S^1) when evaluated on the unit circle S^1. This discovery leads to the conclusion that the set of surjective differential operators H does not include any compact analogues within the context of C^0(S^1). Finally, we demonstrate that for any given p > 1, the set of surjective differential operators H is not compact within the context of C^0(S^1). In addition to these findings, we also establish the relationship between the set of surjective differential operators H and the concept of strong surjectivity, discovering that they are mutually exclusive and equivalent to each other. FedBuff introduces a novel framework that enhances federated learning confidentiality by using fully private data processing, coupled with enhanced confidentiality guarantees for server nodes. To achieve this, the algorithm breaks down complex computations into manageable components, which are then efficiently outsourced to remote servers. Unlike current federated learning methods, FedBuff enables servers to process data using arbitrary neural network structures, not just simple linear models. Unlike current private federated learning approaches, FedBuff provides unconditioned confidentiality guarantees for server nodes, both with and without node recryption. Additionally, the proposed method enhances scalability by minimizing data communication, coupled with improved accuracy through server node involvement. FedBuff's capabilities are demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, revealing its superior performance and scalable design. The code for FedBuff is publicly available at https://github.com/Qianhewu/FedBuff. As the field of federated learning continues to evolve, the current limitations of the FedBuff algorithm provide valuable directions for future research.

In this study, we develop a method to extend the solution existence theorem for relativistic stellar models with two fluids to include solutions derived from those with a single fluid. Specifically, we demonstrate that any solution existing within the interior of a star can be mapped to a corresponding solution for a star composed of a single fluid, made up of the same species of particles as the two-fluid model, provided certain conditions are met. Additionally, we establish that any solution admissible in the $\beta$-parameter space can also be admissible in the single-fluid $\beta$-parameter space. Furthermore, we investigate and compare the properties of two-fluid and single-fluid $n=3$ rotating neutron stars with the same mass and density. Finally, we outline the limitations of our single-fluid model assumptions and discuss possible future directions. Our results contribute to a better understanding of the two-fluid equation of state and its relationship to the single-fluid equation of state. Our approach provides a framework for extending the solution existence theorem to include two-fluid models and demonstrates the utility of this framework through application to specific rotating neutron star scenarios. Our findings also highlight the need for further research into the two-fluid equation of state, particularly using microscopic approaches, and the need for investigations into the two-fluid equation of state for rotating stellar models with other compositions. Our work paves the way for investigating the stability of two-fluid models and rotating two-fluid neutron stars. Offline learning for offline systems is a pressing issue in real-world applications, and it presents a significant challenge for offline ML systems that operate on shared individual trajectories. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework that enables offline learning for multiple agents using shared individual trajectories. Unlike traditional methods that require individual trajectory data for each agent, our framework utilizes a single set of shared individual trajectories for multiple agents. To achieve this, we developed a two-stage approach that first learns a general latent structure from the shared individual trajectories and then incorporates agent-specific latent structures to facilitate efficient offline learning. Our method demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art offline learning techniques for both single-agent and multi-agent systems in extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets in various domains. Notably, our approach surpasses existing benchmarks by significant margins of 13% and 21% in terms of accuracy in single-agent and multi-agent settings, respectively. Furthermore, our approach provides intuitive and visually representable results through dimensionality reduction techniques, showcasing the effectiveness of our method in uncovering underlying patterns and relationships in complex datasets. Our framework and methodical evaluations are available at https://sit.se.

The growing complexity of x-ray scattering experiments stems in part from increasing numbers of detectors, making data processing a significant bottleneck. In x-ray spectroscopy, determining the energy of ejected electrons through phase retrieval is crucial, as it requires solving a nonlinear inverse problem using interferometric data. Existing approaches often rely on starting guesses that can significantly influence outcomes and have limitations in handling large datasets. In response, we've developed a novel algorithm called the Difference Map Method (DMM), which succeeds in accurately reconstructing complex spectra, even with thousands of channels, through a strictly convex optimization process. In our analysis, DMM is compared to current methods, including difference map-based strategies and conventional recursive algorithms. By utilizing Born approximations and validating simulations with realistic data, our research demonstrates the DMM's capability to efficiently handle multi-channel experiments with precise results. In addition, we've applied DMM to real-world data featuring scattered x-rays and ejected energy spectra with remarkable success. In the end, this new algorithmic contribution is poised to enhance the energy resolution of x-ray scattering experiments by significantly reducing computation time to a few seconds. This achievement is crucial for experiments like the 45 kHz time-stamped x-ray spectroscopy currently under development. In such scenarios, where the number of detectors is vast and accurate spectral recovery is crucial, DMM is an ideal solution. This research is an extension of our previous study, where we explored the application of the Difference Map Method to a single, interferometric x-ray energy spectrum. This previous work was based on a linear approximation, whereas the current analysis builds upon that foundation by utilizing a nonlinear, convex optimization process that enables the recovery of more complex spectra. In our initial study, the DMM successfully reconstructed various linear combinations of overlapping peaks within a range of 10:1, accurately identifying all peaks above a certain threshold of confidence. In contrast, the nonlinear DMM can recover more complex spectra consisting of both narrow and broad peaks that are partially overlapped, where the distance between the base of two peaks is at least 20 times the duration of the narrower peak. This capability of the DMM to handle a wider range of spectra is a direct result of the use of a nonlinear convex optimization process. In addition, the DMM has been compared to current phase retrieval algorithms, including the widely used Recursive Regularized Contrast Transfer Function (RRCDF) algorithm and Difference Map-based strategies, in addition to various initial guess strategies. This study introduces a novel numerical approach that leverages the power of deep learning to enhance the efficiency of a common challenge in modeling subsurface geology. By utilizing a directed graph, researchers can represent blocking, complex fractures that intersect each other. A significant blocking fracture that intersects other fractures can be difficult to model using traditional numerical methods due to its extensive degree of freedom. To address this issue, a mechanism known as the Dirac-β approach has gained popularity in recent years. Nonetheless, the approach requires a substantial amount of time to compute the gradient of the Euclidean distance function, thereby limiting its scalability. To overcome this computation challenge, a sample-based approach has been proposed, but it comes with a significant increase in parameters and training time. A more efficient solution was proposed, but it is limited to modeling single-block fractures. In contrast, the present study introduces a blocking fracture approach that utilizes a graph convolutional neural network (GCNN) to compute the Dirac-β approach's gradient by approximating the gradient of the Euclidean distance function. The research team demonstrated the effectiveness and efficiency of their novel approach by modeling a realistic blocking fracture that measures 100x100 nodes, a large and complex geometry that is equivalent to approximately 10,000 linear dimensions, with a notable reduction in computation time. The study's contribution lies in its capability to efficiently model blocking fractures that intersect each other, and the resulting code framework is available for public use, offering users a flexible and highly efficient solution for modeling intricate geologies. The code framework's name is BlockFractureGCNN. We investigate the geometric characteristics of the factorized objective in matrix optimization, specifically focusing on the geodesic convexity of the natural Newton scheme. To do this, we examine the restricted strong convexity and smoothness of the objective function. Our findings demonstrate that the factorized objective exhibits nonmonotonic geodesic behavior. To illustrate the implications of this behavior, we establish the convergence of the natural Newton scheme using a backward error perspective. This approach highlights the connection to the nonmonotone geodesic convexity of the factorized objective. We also establish the relationship between the natural parameters and the augmented Lagrangian method. To facilitate the analysis of the augmented Lagrangian method, we introduce a new concept: the relative distance between two matrices. This leads to the development of a new inequality, which we refer to as the ``relative mean curvature inequality''. This inequality provides a lower bound on the mean curvature inequality and has been previously used in the context of the natural Newton scheme. To demonstrate the applicability of this inequality, we examine the natural Newton scheme and the augmented Lagrangian method. Finally, we conclude by discussing the limitations of the current research on the geodesic convexity of the natural Newton scheme and the augmented Lagrangian method. Our study on the relative mean curvature inequality and the associated inequality for the augmented Lagrangian method can be found in the additional file. This additional file contains a further investigation of the mean curvature inequality and its application to the natural Newton scheme and the augmented Lagrangian method. It also includes an overview of the main results presented in the current study. In 1990, Faudree and Schelp proposed an unconfirmed hypothesis: any bipartite graph with a maximum edge degree of 3 can be thoroughly colored using four colors, except for a minor adjustment to account for a specific pattern of parallel edges. We have successfully proven this conjecture in its adjusted form, demonstrating that the Faudree-Schelp construction, which includes a specific set of bipartite graphs with maximum edge degree 3, requires six edge colors, although this requirement can be reduced to four edge colors by modifying the graph pattern. Additionally, we have proven that the optimal edge coloring for the Faudree-Schelp construction, which includes a specific set of bipartite graphs with maximum edge degree 3, requires five edge colors. These achievements represent significant advancements in resolving the Faudree-Schelp conjecture, particularly in regards to ear-decomposition methods. In the process of addressing this conjecture, we have also successfully colored certain complex graphs using five edge colors, thereby confirming the Faudree-Schelp conjecture in its original form. In the course of our research, we have also provided edge coloring proofs for two specific types of graphs that have major components described as'stars' and 'wheels', demonstrating that these graphs can be thoroughly colored using four edge colors, except for a minor adjustment to account for a specific pattern of parallel edges. Moreover, we have proven that the optimal edge coloring for a specific type of wheel graph, which includes a central node connected to several outer nodes, requires the same number of edge colors as its maximum edge degree, thereby confirming that this wheel graph can be thoroughly colored using three edge colors. Furthermore, we have also confirmed that the optimal edge coloring for a specific type of tree graph, which includes a central node connected to two outer nodes, connected to other tree components, requires the same number of edge colors as its maximum edge degree, except for a minor adjustment to account for a specific pattern of parallel edges, thereby thoroughly coloring the tree graph using two edge colors, except for a minor adjustment to account for a specific pattern of parallel edges. In the process of addressing this conjecture, we have also provided edge coloring proofs for several other complex graphs, including a grape graph, a thumb joint graph, a join of two star graphs, a join of two wheel graphs, and a chain of two star graphs, demonstrating that these graphs can be thoroughly colored using five edge colors, except for a minor adjustment to account for a specific pattern of parallel edges. This study investigates the co-evolutionary dynamics of genetic algorithms in two scenarios: individual learning and social learning. Our analysis focuses on the Hamming distance between solutions generated and an optimal Nash Equilibrium (NE). Our results show that in the context of NE, the Hamming distance exhibits an inverse relationship with system fitness. Our data also reveal distinct learning curves for individual and social learning systems. In particular, we observe that in the initial stages, the expected Hamming distance from a Nash Equilibrium exhibits similar growth patterns in both learning scenarios. By contrast, the Hamming distance in the social learning case surpasses the individual learning variant at a rate proportional to the product of its population size and the number of iterations. Our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the co-evolutionary dynamics of genetic algorithms through a unique combination of analytical and simulation-based approaches. Our findings highlight the performance enhancements achievable through optimal strategy selection and highlight the potential applications of this research in fields such as social learning and complex systems study. Our simulation code is available in the repository https://github.com/ChengLi2020/EGAN. Consider a weighted oriented graph, denoted as $G$, with edge ideal $R_G$ and power $e_G^n$, where $n$ represents the index. We demonstrate that $R_G^{(n)} \cong \gamma(R_G)^n$ and $R_G^{(n)} \cong \gamma^s(R_G)^n$ for any $n$, where $\gamma$ and $\gamma^s$ signify the ordinary and symbolic Frobenius operators, respectively. Additionally, we establish that $e_G^{(n)}$ equals $\gamma^s(e_G)^n$ or $\gamma(e_G)^n$ with generation properties, depending on the structure of $G$. Moreover, we discover that the Koszul complexity of $R_G^{(n)}$ remains unchanged at $n$, whereas the linear strand of $R_G^{(n)}$ deepens to $n$ levels, where $n$ refers to the index. We also examine the relationship between $R_G^{(n)}$ and the polynomial ring $k[x_1,\ldots,x_m]$ following a specific ordering, known as the lexicographic ordering with weights, which we call ERO (Earley's Ordering). We prove that $R_G^{(n)}$ equals the ring defined by ERO, thereby establishing its equidimensional property. Moreover, we demonstrate that the depth of $R_G^{(n)}$ reaches $n$ when the edge ideal $R_G$ possesses a linear strand of depth $n$. We also investigate the relationship between the Koszul complexity and the ERO ordering of $R_G^{(n)}$. By describing the minimal generators of $\gamma^s(e_G)^n$ and $\gamma(e_G)^n$, we conclude the paper. We acknowledge that our study involves contributing to the theory of weighted oriented graphs, particularly with regard to power operations on edge ideals. Furthermore, we highlight the advantages of using the ordinary and symbolic Frobenius operators in this context. We also emphasize the significance of the equidimensional property, which arises from considering power operations on edge ideals. Moreover, we point out the value of evaluating power operations on edge ideals in relation to the Koszul complexity and the ERO ordering. We acknowledge the expertise of various mathematicians whose contributions have paved the way for our research in this area. We also thank the reviewers for their valuable feedback on our work. We acknowledge the financial support we received to conduct this research.

Neural networks are susceptible to subtle errors caused by hardware malfunctions, leading to compromised performance. To mitigate this issue, we propose a method called Uniform Quantization Checking to enforce consistent data representation across layers in neural networks, ensuring the accuracy of their predictions. However, implementing uniform quantization constraints on networks that use non-uniform data representations poses a challenge. To address this issue, we introduce a distinct checking framework for non-uniform constraints, resulting in a more general method that encompasses uniform quantization checking. Our experiments with real-world datasets demonstrate that neural networks with non-uniform data representations, when subject to our checking method, exhibit a significant decrease in the error of their predictions, with some cases showing a 6.5% increase in their correct classification rate when classified using a rigorous setting. Moreover, our experiments show that the existing uniform constraint checking technique is insufficient for tackling the problem of silent data corruption in neural networks, leading us to conclude that a more comprehensive checking method is necessary. We have publicly available code and datasets for reproducibility purposes.

Recently, the generalization of the Jordanian twist was formulated and the corresponding star product was derived for a specific Lie algebra. This paper extends those findings to all bosonic Serre Lie algebras and provides the generalization of the Jordanian twist in $d$-dimensions. It then determines the corresponding star product and shows that it converges rapidly. Notably, it demonstrates that the generalization of the simple Jordanian twist equals the universal Jordanian twist, thereby establishing a direct relationship between these two twists. Additionally, it demonstrates that the generalization of the Jordanian twist leads to the same differential equation as the simple Jordanian twist, thereby confirming that they behave similarly. Furthermore, it proposes a straightforward approach to applying the Jordanian twist to the $r$-matrix and explores its connection to the dynamical Wigner-Weyl transformation. Finally, it outlines the implications of using the Jordanian twist in the AdS/CFT context. The resulting star product can be utilized to solve the conformal field equation in the presence of a cosmological constant. The solution to this equation is intriguing and may be linked to the Birkhoff conjecture. The research presented in this paper was conducted as part of the Ph.D. studies at the University of Lyon under the guidance of H. G. Estabroso. The findings have been partially published in the paper "Generalized Jordanian twist and simple twist equivalence" that appeared in the Journal of Physics, Mathcentral, and arXiv notes. To further improve the model's performance, the study introduces a novel embedding technique called directional embedding, which is an extension of the existing word embedding methods. Our research analyzed recent measurements of particle ratios from ALICE, ATLAS, and CMS for the most commonly studied hadrons and electrons, examining their behavior across different collision systems from proton-proton to lead-lead collisions. We observed that medium-weight ion collisions exhibit phenomena similar to both light ion and heavy ion collisions, yet the uncertainty associated with current data is too great to definitively determine these trends. Nonetheless, previous studies suggesting a scaling of particle production with the number of participant nucleons in deep inelastic scattering and fixed-target collisions are consistent with newer data. We further investigated these phenomena by fitting individual hadron equations and calculating probability distributions of model parameter variations. These results provide a basis for extending existing hadron production models to next-generation experiments involving new collision energies and kinematic ranges. Additionally, we identified opportunities for improving current models through greater accuracy. Ultimately, more precise particle ratios in medium-weight ion collisions will be necessary for accurately scaling existing hadron production models to those collision systems. Our analysis has implications for future experiments at the Large Hadron Collider and the Large Solid Angle Experiment (LHC-S) that will facilitate further study of hadron physics in heavy-ion collisions. In addition, we outline potential paths for model developments that could enhance hadron generation in experiments involving future collision machines. Furthermore, we outline the importance of accurately generating hadron physics in future heavy-ion collisions, not just for particle-level analysis but also for jet hadronization in quantum chromodynamics. This research paves the way for extending existing hadron generation models to newer data and different experiments, and highlights the value of thoroughly testing hadron generation within experimental collaborations. This research is also relevant to ongoing and future experiments involving heavy-ion collisions, as it provides a foundation for developing more advanced hadron generation models.
