Although this model accurately predicts numerous astronomical constants, it falls short in its physical explanations. The proposed model also lacks an intuitive basis for its viscosity concept, primarily due to the lack of an underlying mechanism. A new model is presented, built on the proposal but with an alternative interpretation of the viscosity coefficient, which is now a function of time rather than a constant. This time-dependent approach provides a possible underlying mechanism for the model, albeit one that is fundamentally different from the conventional understanding of viscosity as a result of particle interactions. This new model retains the accuracy it had for the astronomical constants, while also making predictions for previously unaccounted physical properties of the ground state energy of space. A calculation of the expected value of the square of the energy density of the ground state shows that the model's prediction aligns with the energy density observed in the quantum vacuum, with an error margin of less than 0.3%. A comparison with existing research reveals that this new model offers a viscosity-like concept that is more intimately connected to the energy spectrum of the ground state, rather than a fixed quantity. A proposal for determining the model's parameters through electromagnetic interference data from an particle accelerator is also presented. A proposed experiment for testing the model's time-dependent viscosity prediction by measuring the scattering width of the ground state energy fluctuation (zero-point motion) is also outlined. A calculation of this scattering width with the new model indicates that it is extremely sensitive to the viscosity-like parameter, and could potentially be accurate enough to reveal the viscosity-like aspect of zero-point motion during a future experiment. Our approach is distinguished from other alternating direction methods by utilizing a second-order model to approximate the smooth component. Our method is developed under the guidance of a proximal gradient framework, which enables the inclusion of additional regularization techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of MFSSA by conducting numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world data. We investigate a random walk with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) components that have a mean of zero. Our research explores the long-term behavior of this random walk as it exceeds a significant threshold, beyond which its asymptotic properties can be either driven by its largest component or governed by more complex dynamics. To examine this, we divide the components into two groups: one with significant increments and a second with smaller increments. We analyze the random walk's asymptotic behavior in different regimes, defined by the ratio of its largest component to the mean of its smaller components. Our findings reveal that for certain conditions, the random walk's asymptotic properties are similar to those of the largest component, whereas in other cases, they mirror those of the smaller components. Our study also reveals distinct patterns of dynamics, including systems that can switch between different asymptotic behaviors or exhibit more intricate patterns of self-similarity. Our research provides a framework for understanding various generalizations and identifies relationships between distinct regimes with different dynamics. This study introduces a novel W-shaped network to achieve a higher level of performance in detecting cell nuclei in cervical cancer screening, surpassing competitors by a significant margin. Our proposed framework, consisting of two branches with opposing functions, reduces image processing data by directing irrelevant information away from the main pathway, thereby significantly enhancing efficiency. To further improve performance, a multi-scale approach is implemented, and the network is modified to output multiple probabilities, resulting in our proposal being ranked first in the 2013 Cervical Cancer Screening Challenge. When applied to a more challenging dataset, it demonstrates the ability to detect nuclei in images with overlapping objects and varied backgrounds, showcasing the framework's versatility. The code for our W-shaped network is available on GitHub. When compared to state-of-the-art competitors on the 2013 challenge, it achieved a score of 9.907, and on the more challenging FFER dataset, a score of 84.441 was attained after fine-tuning. Our approach provides a significant advantage over existing methods with similar efficiency, as determined by model size and processing time. This advantage comes with little compromise in performance, as demonstrated by our results in cervical cancer screening. This approach has the potential to be applied to other medical image detection tasks. The code for our W-shaped network is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zuoyi-1992/W-shaped-network. The code can be used as a baseline for other nucleus detection projects, and it is intended to be used with the PyTorch deep learning framework, which can be obtained from https://www.pytorch.org/. This understanding allows us to reframe classic problems such as image recognition and handwriting identification as applications of GCNs. We have discovered that by assigning a graph to the problem in question and training a GCN on that graph, we can replicate the results obtained from the original CNN and fully connected Neural Network approaches. What's more, this GCN-based implementation yields transparent representations of the problem's structural features, which can be utilized for additional analyses. We have further demonstrated that this GCN implementation can be used to accomplish feature extraction for other machine learning algorithms, thereby leveraging the benefits of both GCNs and traditional Neural Networks. A fundamental challenge in elastography arises from the uncertainty surrounding the direction of sound wave propagation, which makes axial and lateral tissue displacement estimates equally prone to $90^\circ$ measurement errors.  As a result, the more accurate axial displacement estimate is often used to calculate tissue stiffness in current elastography methods.  Despite this limitation, research has shown that using lateral displacement estimates can lead to better image quality and more accurate stiffness measurements.  With this motivation in mind, this paper develops a static contrast enhancement technique based on the Caruso equation that takes into account both axial and lateral particle displacement ratios, which are estimated from B-mode images using a new autoregressive model.  The proposed method takes advantage of its ability to utilize displacement estimates from axially-oriented scans to create more accurate images of tissue structure by incorporating lateral displacement estimates.  The results of experiments conducted on real elastography data subjects reveal that the proposed technique outperforms current methods in various metrics, including contrast-to-noise ratio, absolute contrast, and root mean square contrast, which can serve as precursors for modeling tissue stiffness. In 1936, G. E. Moore delivered a lecture where he strengthened Godel's first incompleteness theorem by showing that any sufficiently powerful formal system that is capable of describing itself must contain a statement that is neither provable nor refutable within the system, yet has a counterpart among the system's valid statements that can be accessed through intuition. However, Moore's enhancement of Godel's theorem was presented without the accompanying proof that has been lost over time. We aim to revive the understanding of this significant concept by providing a modern interpretation of the underlying ideas and the missing proof for the benefit of current mathematical thinkers. We also introduce the concept of "anti-formulas" which we believe has value beyond the context of the theorem. Additionally, we offer a straightforward proof of the enhanced version of the first incompleteness theorem that is consistent with the principles of Godel's original argument, while simplifying the existing proof frameworks. We also tackle some of the criticisms that have been raised against the incompleteness theorems over the years. We then delve into the relationship between the enhanced first incompleteness theorem and the concept of undecidability in the context of the halting problem, as well as the connection to the idea that any formal system cannot contain all meaningful logical statements. Furthermore, we explore the implications of the enhanced first incompleteness theorem on the fundamental nature of mathematics and the potential limitations of artificial intelligence systems that are based on formal foundations. We also examine some possible interpretations of the statement that there are logical statements that are neither provable nor refutable within a given formal system, nor can they be determined to be meaningful or meaningless, despite being part of the system's intended meaning. We conclude by considering some of the possible reasons why the concept of the enhanced first incompleteness theorem has not gained the attention it deserves in the mathematical community over the years. We hope that our work will revive the interest of mathematicians and logicians in this significant and captivating aspect of the incompleteness theorems that has far-reaching implications for various branches of mathematics and computer science. We also hope that our introduction of the concept of "anti-formulas" will find value in its own right within the mathematical community. We would like to emphasize that the enhanced first incompleteness theorem is not seen as a refinement of the original Godel's first incompleteness theorem but rather an extension of its underlying ideas, which has a deeper significance. The model's structure, previously applied to analyze non-speech biological signals, is thought to mimic the brain's physiological signal processing, with short-term frequency analysis and longer periodic time-domain processing achieved through the reservoir and recurrent units within each module. The model's success can be attributed to its minimal parameter count rather than its complex structure, as proven by a parametric equivalent evaluation. Identifying the source of audio within a complex real-world scenario is a difficult problem. Due to the diversity of audio contexts, developing efficient methods requires robust, context-agnostic technology. To accelerate sound source separation research, a comprehensive dataset is crucial, given the current limitations of existing datasets. Our proposed solution addresses these challenges with the VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) benchmark. VGG-SS is a comprehensive sound source separation dataset spanning multiple contexts, consisting of 12 distinct sources and a unique aspect - it allows for context-agnostic modeling by excluding background information in half of the samples. With over 12 hours of diverse audio for each source and 240 hours of training data, VGG-SS sets a new standard for small-domain sound source separation datasets. Our solution achieves state-of-the-art performance in four challenging, small-domain datasets and provides contextual-agnostic models for future sound source separation research. Our code and dataset are available for public use at https://github.com/Vggopt/VGG-SS.

This paper introduces Lorentzian Graph Convolutional Network (LGCN), a novel hyperbolic convolutional neural network, which enhances existing hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) in representing node features. Our research finds that while hyperbolic GCNs can efficiently reduce the dimensional complexity of graph-structured data, they struggle to effectively capture local structure information, primarily due to the limited ability of their convolutional modules to accurately learn non-linear transformations in high-dimensional spaces. To address this challenge, LGCN leverages a unique combination of geometric learning and relation aggregation techniques to enhance the capacity of hyperbolic GCNs. Specifically, we develop a Lorentzian-based convolutional module with adjustable non-linear transformation and a tree-based graph decomposition method to enhance learning efficiency and accuracy. Additionally, a global relation aggregation module and a new multi-scale relation learning technique are introduced to facilitate the exchange of information among distinct representation learning processes and the exploration of local and global structure properties simultaneously. Our LGCN achieves significant performance enhancements over existing hyperbolic GCNs in various large-scale citation network and protein interaction network datasets, demonstrating its robustness and versatility. This work also provides an intuitive explanation of LGCN's behavior using hyperspace visualization of learned representations. The Tsallis distribution has extensive applications in various fields, and the Pareto distribution, a specific case of Tsallis distribution, has been widely observed in social systems. We propose a new explanation for the Tsallis distribution's presence in decision-making processes that involve randomness, such as the distribution of voters' ranks in democratic systems. We demonstrate that when individuals randomly select others to look up for advice, the resulting Tsallis distribution of authorities' ranks aligns with existing observational data. This phenomenon is robust across different population sizes, variance of random choice, and connection strength. Furthermore, our findings show that the Tsallis distribution's parameters reflect the characteristics of the system, allowing them to serve as indicators for measuring the effectiveness of random choice in achieving fair distribution. We also observe that the Tsallis distribution evolves in time, reflecting changes in the system's characteristics, and that it can be accurate even when the underlying distribution is non-pareto, even non-tsallisian. We provide a theoretical framework for understanding the Tsallis distribution in large-scale settings and present numerical results that demonstrate its applicability. For quantum equilibrium states on a lattice system, four types of Hamiltonian dynamics have been identified: scaling, extending, reducing, and invariant dynamics. This study examines local quantum equilibrium (LQE) situations and demonstrates that their generating operators belong to the scaling dynamics category. Furthermore, by using the concept of local quantum equilibrium, conditions for Wigner-Pauli-Hausdorff scaling dynamics have been established. These conditions are necessary for the scaling dynamics to be considered valid. Additionally, it has been proven that the scaling dynamics is invariant if, for any local observable, the average with respect to the equilibrium state is zero. A crucial aspect of this result is that it does not rely on the assumption of decaying correlations. Nevertheless, it is noted that in one-dimensional chains with a strict sublattice connection, all Wigner-Pauli-Hausdorff scaling dynamics are invariant. Nevertheless, this is not the case for certain classic examples in higher dimensions. Moreover, it is emphasized that the invariance of scaling dynamics provides more precise information than the distinction between increasing and decreasing dynamics. Indeed, the concept of negative temperature is often misinterpreted due to the incorrect analogy with classical temperatures, which has led some to believe that it's impossible to achieve negative temperature in two-level systems. However, using the population inversion example, we can illustrate that negative temperature is simply a matter of non-zero difference between the two energy levels. Consequently, incorporating decoherence effects into the standard two-level system model reveals that negative temperature can be shown through simple harmonic oscillator analogies. Ultimately, this model decomposes into a series of coupled harmonic oscillators, allowing us to gain insight into the concept of negative temperature within two-level systems. Furthermore, it provides a clear, non-ambiguous representation of negative temperature based on the frequency spacing between the energy levels. This representation can be experimentally verified through phase-dependent studies during decoherence processes involving two-level systems. Moreover, this approach highlights the importance of distinguishing between the thermostat and system levels, which is particularly crucial when discussing negative temperature. Finally, this two-level system model serves as a concise, yet comprehensive, representation of the concept and physical implications of negative temperature. Moreover, it can be applied to a wide range of experimental scenarios, including quantum dots, NMR systems, and superconducting qubits. Ultimately, this model demonstrates the value of two-level system models in illustrating the negative temperature phenomena with physical analogies that are easily understandable, while also providing a precise, experimental-proof-based representation. A comprehensive theoretical analysis of the effective spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides is presented, with a focus on understanding how interaction effects and crystal field splitting influence this quantity. The approach involves utilizing a general perturbation theory to derive the effective spin-orbit coupling from the spin-orbit coupling and crystal field within the framework of multi-orbital Hubbard models. A key finding shows that the effective spin-orbit coupling exhibits a non-trivial relationship with the filling level, crystal field splitting, and electron-electron interaction strengths. It is also observed that in some cases the effective spin-orbit coupling can take on a sign opposite to the original quantity. This approach is particularly applicable to transition metal oxides with strong spin-orbit coupling and intermediate electron filling levels. To illustrate the methodology's relevance and accuracy, the effective spin-orbit coupling is calculated for both Sr$_2$TaO$_4$ and Ca$_2$TaO$_4$, showing excellent agreement with experimental results as well as previous theoretical analyses. Additionally, a dimensionless spin-orbit entropy is introduced to differentiate between localized and itinerant spin-orbit coupled behaviors. Lastly, a parameter that determines the itinerant or localized nature of spin-orbit behavior is obtained from the effective mass calculation, allowing for a comparison with this entropy and the filling level's dependence on the fillings. The findings provide a clear understanding of how interaction effects and crystal field splitting influence the spin-orbit coupled behavior in transition metal oxides, offering a theoretical framework that can be utilized to study other materials featuring strong spin-orbit coupling and intermediate electron fillings. The approach's itinerant characterization is supported by a comparison with both local and itinerant spin-orbit coupled behaviors and involves a effective mass calculation that differentiates these behaviors. The findings also show that the effective spin-orbit entropy can distinguish between itinerant and localized spin-orbit coupled behaviors. Preceding the expressiveness of $A$-hypergeometric functions, relative $I$-functions from toric complete intersections with smooth divisors serve as a fundamental building block. These relative $I$-functions demonstrate uniqueness, as they are distinguished by their distinct periods. However, the majority of relative $I$-functions share a common characteristic - they can be expressed as products of certain basic relative $I$-functions associated with hypergeometric functions. We aim to establish that when a toric complete intersection possesses a specific property, its relative $I$-function can be factorized into a product of basic relative $I$-functions in a specific order, reflecting the hierarchy of its defining polynomials. Furthermore, when a toric complete intersection possesses another property, its relative $I$-function remains invariant under a specific transformation, and this phenomenon is observed in cases where the intersection varies, yet the underlying relative $I$-function remains the same. We will also explore and classify these invariants relative $I$-functions. Specifically, we will provide an extensive list of such functions associated with hypergeometric functions, including notable examples such as the Gauss hypergeometric function, the Appell function, the Struve function, the Legendre function, the hypergeometric function of three variables, as well as certain systems of hypergeometric functions. Ultimately, our study seeks to establish a direct connection between these relative $I$-functions and the underlying geometry of toric complete intersections. Consequently, we can approximate the periods of relative $I$-functions as a result of integrating hypergeometric functions, thereby facilitating the generation of $A$-hypergeometric functions from an infinite array of periods parameterized by varieties of toric complete intersections. We will demonstrate the applicability and utility of this framework by generating the periods required for the computation of relative $I$-functions associated with specific hypergeometric functions, including the Gauss hypergeometric function and the Appell function of first type. By exploring the relationship between relative $I$-functions and hypergeometric functions, we can establish the legitimacy of certain varieties of toric complete intersections as sources of periods for hypergeometric functions. In turn, this insight enables us to enhance the expressiveness of $A$-hypergeometric functions by gaining access to an infinite array of periods parameterized by varieties of toric complete intersections. We will also investigate the consequences of this finding for the theory of $A$-hypergeometric functions.

Using generative models to modify internal representations of images can lead to a deeper understanding of how medical conditions are represented. This approach enables investigation of whether the model's representation of a specific image label is accurate by examining the generated image and reporting any discrepancies. We employed this technique to explore the representations of lung health in CT scans by manipulating the label from healthy to ill and comparing the resulting image with known pathological changes. Our primary goal was to identify whether the model's representation of lung health is simply a binary code based on the presence or absence of specific lesions, or if it includes additional information such as inflammation located in different parts of the lung. However, due to the limitations of the current approach, we were unable to distinguish between a categorical and a quantitative code. Nonetheless, we discovered that a model using a latent code can accurately reflect the complexity of a medical condition like lung health by considering multiple factors. To demonstrate this, we extracted the latent code associated with the lung region to produce a sorted list of the most influential factors, or "weights", which revealed detailed information about the disease, including its distribution and severity. Consequently, this method can be a valuable tool for investigating how medical conditions are represented in images by using generative models. To this end, we have developed an framework that enables code manipulation for a broad range of medical image classifications and provides a visually interpretable representation of the corresponding code, which we have made available for download. Our results are further illustrated in the accompanying video. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ghiba/medical-latent-code. Our work has implications for using generative models in clinical settings, where they could be used to quantify the severity of a medical condition by analyzing internal representations of image features. This approach could also be applied to other types of images and classifications. We have presented our findings to the computational community and plan to present them to the medical community in the future. ViDaExpert is an advanced data visualization tool designed to facilitate the exploration of complex data sets consisting of multiple variables. This user-friendly interface can display high-dimensional data using interactive 3D plots, allowing for the investigation of relationships between different variables. Furthermore, it includes features for identifying the most significant variables and interacting with the plots to gain deeper insights. In this research, ViDaExpert is utilized to analyze a real-world dataset of art pieces, discovering underlying patterns and distinguishing features. The results demonstrate that this tool effectively uncovers the most important variables, thereby providing a straightforward solution for uncovering dimensionality in large datasets. The code and application of ViDaExpert are available online. In particular, the development of a classification system for Madonna paintings serves as the underlying problem being investigated. In this example, ViDaExpert identifies the most significant variables governing artistic style, thereby establishing a foundation for precise classification methods. The associated data and analysis instructions can be found in the supplementary materials.
